ALPHABET = '123456789ABCDEFGHJKLMNPQRSTUVWXYZabcdefghijkmnopqrstuvwxyz'
def b58(data):
    n = int.from_bytes(data, 'big')
    out = ''
    while n:
        n, r = divmod(n, 58)
        out = ALPHABET[r] + out
    zeros = len(data) - len(data.lstrip(b'\x00'))

title: Digital signatures: SIGHASH, schnorr and ECDSA, recomputed against the standards and Bitcoin Core 31.1

nodes.label: Foundations of digital signatures
nodes.body: A digital signature is the proof that the person who controls a private key has authorized a transaction, and this branch collects what the chapter's first sections say about it: the three jobs of a signature (authorization by the owner, non-repudiation and integrity of the signed data), the numbers it is computed with, and the fact that each input of a transaction carries its own independent signature. It matters because every payment on the blockchain stands or falls with a signature check, and the check needs only the message, the public key and the signature. The branch is verified by running the chapter's implementation of ECDSA and schnorr, built on the curve arithmetic of chapter 4, and by comparing the results with Bitcoin Core (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.label: What a signature does
nodes.body: This group states what a signature verification needs and promises: three inputs, the answer yes only if they belong together, and the three purposes the book names, which are authorization, non-repudiation and integrity (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.label: Inputs of verification
nodes.body: A digital signature is checked by a verification function that takes three inputs: the message that was signed (in Bitcoin, a hash of a chosen part of the transaction), the public key of the signer, and the signature itself, and it answers yes or no. The chapter's script runs this with a test key and gets yes for the matching trio and no when the message is replaced by another, when the public key is replaced by another, or when the signature is replaced by one made with a different private key, which is the list [True, False, False, False]. This is why a node needs no secret and no connection to the signer to validate a payment: everything it needs is published in the transaction and in the output being spent (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
nodes.definition: A verifier needs exactly three inputs, the message, the public key and the signature, and the answer is yes only when all three belong together.

nodes.label: Integrity of the message
nodes.body: The third of the three purposes the book gives a digital signature is integrity: after the signer has signed, nobody can change the signed data without the change being noticed. The chapter's script signs a 32-byte digest, flips a single bit of it and verifies again, and the answer is False. In a Bitcoin transaction this means that once a spender has signed with the common flag SIGHASH_ALL, a miner or a relay node cannot redirect the payment to another address or change the amount, because the signature would no longer verify against the changed transaction (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
nodes.example: one flipped bit in the message
nodes.definition: A signature covers its message, so changing even one bit of the message makes the signature fail.

nodes.label: Binding to the key
nodes.body: The first purpose is authorization by the owner of the funds: the output being spent names a public key (or its hash), and only the holder of the matching private key can produce a signature that verifies against it. In the chapter's script a signature made with one private key is checked against the public key of the next private key along and the answer is False. The second purpose, which the book calls non-repudiation, follows because nobody else could have produced the signature and so the proof of authorization is undeniable; the scripts of chapter 7 are what ask the question 'does this signature verify for this key', and this chapter is what answers it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
nodes.example: a signature checked against a neighbour's key
nodes.definition: A signature verifies only against the public key that matches the private key that made it, which is what ties a spend to the owner of the coins.

nodes.label: Arithmetic of the curve
nodes.body: This group concerns the numbers that signature equations use, in particular the two different moduli of the curve and the round trip of signing and verifying, which the chapter's plain-Python implementation passes before any comparison with other software (Wuille et al., 2020).

nodes.label: Scalars are reduced modulo n
nodes.body: Modular arithmetic keeps numbers inside a fixed range by taking remainders, and Bitcoin uses two different moduli on the curve secp256k1: the prime p, which bounds the coordinates of points, and the order n, the number of points in the group generated by G, which bounds the scalars that multiply points. The book says that multiplications in the signature equations are performed modulo p; the executed check shows that this is not what a signature uses. With a test key, a nonce and a large challenge, the value s reduced modulo n makes the equation sG = kG + eX hold (True), the same value reduced modulo p makes it fail (False), and the two numbers are different (True), with p larger than n by more than 2 to the 128. The reason is that multiplying a point by n gives the point at infinity, so scalars repeat with period n and not with period p (Wuille et al., 2020) (SECG, 2010).
nodes.example: the group order n against the field prime p
nodes.definition: The numbers in a signature equation (nonce, challenge, private key, response) are reduced modulo the order n of the curve's group, not modulo the field prime p that the book names.

nodes.label: Sign and verify round trip
nodes.body: The simplest test of any signature implementation is the round trip: sign a message with a private key, verify with the matching public key and expect yes. The chapter builds ECDSA and BIP340 schnorr from the curve arithmetic of chapter 4 in plain Python and starts every demonstration with this round trip, which gives True; the later tests then ask whether the library also agrees with independent software, namely the 19 official BIP340 test vectors, the 500 signature hash vectors of Bitcoin Core and the signatures that Bitcoin Core 31.1 makes on a private test network (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
nodes.definition: Signing with a private key and verifying with the public key returns yes, the basic round trip every signature scheme must satisfy.

nodes.label: Remainder of a division
nodes.body: Every equation of the chapter is computed modulo a number, and the book explains the idea with one sentence: if the modulus were 3 and an operation gave 5, the number actually used is 2, because 5 divided by 3 has a remainder of 2 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The example computes that remainder with the percent operator and the whole quotient with the double slash, giving the pair (2, 1), and the reader can change the number and the modulus to see the remainder wrap around like the hand of a clock that returns to its start after twelve hours. In Bitcoin the modulus is not 3 but a prime of 256 bits for coordinates and the order of the group for scalars, and the next examples use a modulus of 101 so that every step can still be checked by hand.
nodes.definition: Reducing a number modulo m keeps only the remainder of its division by m, so 5 modulo 3 is 2, which is the book's own example of what modulus means.

nodes.label: Signing a transaction
nodes.body: This group concerns what is signed in a transaction: a digest computed from selected fields, signed separately for every input, so that different owners can contribute their own signatures to one transaction (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.label: Independent signatures per input
nodes.body: A transaction can spend several coins at once, and each coin (input) carries its own signature made with the key that owns that coin. The book notes that inputs of different owners can be signed in a partially constructed transaction; the chapter's script builds a transaction with two inputs owned by two different keys, lets each owner sign only their own input with SIGHASH_ALL, and verifies both, then swaps the signatures and finds that both fail. The list [True, True, False, False] shows why: the message each owner signs is the transaction as seen from their own input, so a signature is bound to its input as well as to its key (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
nodes.example: two owners, two inputs, one transaction
nodes.definition: Each input of a transaction is signed separately, so owners of different inputs can sign the same transaction one after the other and neither signature can be moved to the other input.

nodes.label: The signed digest
nodes.body: A signature in Bitcoin is made not over the transaction bytes themselves but over a 32-byte digest computed from them by the signature hash algorithm, and the SIGHASH flag selects which fields go into the digest. The chapter's script computes the legacy digest of a transaction with two inputs and two outputs twice and gets the same value (True), then changes the amount of one output by one satoshi and gets a different value (False for equality), which is the whole mechanism of commitment: a field that is in the digest cannot change after signing, and a field that is not in the digest can (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Bitcoin Wiki, 2026).
nodes.example: changing an output changes the signed hash
nodes.definition: What a signature signs is a hash computed from selected fields of the transaction, so changing a committed field changes the hash and breaks the signature.

nodes.label: Signature hash flags (SIGHASH)
nodes.body: A signature does not have to cover the whole transaction: the SIGHASH flag, one byte at the end of the signature, selects which inputs and outputs the signed hash commits to, and this lets several people build one transaction together, for example a crowdfunding payment to which strangers add inputs. This branch collects the flag values, what each flag commits to (found by changing one field at a time), the known pitfall of SIGHASH_SINGLE and the agreement of the chapter's implementation with Bitcoin Core's 500 test vectors and with signatures that Bitcoin Core 31.1 made with every flag (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

nodes.label: How flags are coded
nodes.body: This group gives the numbers of the flags: the six combinations of ECDSA, the extra default value of taproot, the seven valid taproot hash types and the proposed ANYPREVOUT values, each read from a standard or from Bitcoin Core's header file (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

nodes.label: Flag values
nodes.body: A SIGHASH flag is a single byte appended to a signature that says which parts of the transaction the signature covers. The base flags are ALL (1), NONE (2) and SINGLE (3), and the modifier ANYONECANPAY has the value 0x80, which is 128, so that it combines with each base flag by addition to give 129, 130 and 131, written 0x81, 0x82 and 0x83 in hexadecimal. The chapter's library lists them as [1, 2, 3, 128, 129, 130, 131], the values of the book's tables, and the next leaf shows that Bitcoin Core's source declares the same constants (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). In the partially signed transaction format that wallets pass between signers, each input can name the type its signature must use in the field PSBT_IN_SIGHASH_TYPE, key type 0x03 (Chow, 2017).
nodes.definition: The three base flags are the numbers 1, 2 and 3 and ANYONECANPAY adds 0x80, which gives the six combinations 1, 2, 3, 129, 130 and 131.

nodes.label: Constants in Bitcoin Core
nodes.body: The reference for what the network accepts is the code of Bitcoin Core, so the chapter reads the constants from the saved copy of src/script/interpreter.h at the pinned commit: SIGHASH_ALL = 1, SIGHASH_NONE = 2, SIGHASH_SINGLE = 3, SIGHASH_ANYONECANPAY = 0x80, and a fifth constant SIGHASH_DEFAULT = 0 whose comment says it is for taproot only, is implied when the sighash byte is missing and is equivalent to SIGHASH_ALL. The list [1, 2, 3, 128, 0] is what the script reads, and the zero is the value the book's table does not have, because the book's table is about ECDSA signatures (Bitcoin Core, 2026). This example reads core_src_script_interpreter.h, a file saved with the chapter's evidence (the fetched sources, their test vectors or the record of Bitcoin Core 31.1.0's run), and a browser does not have it. Recorded output, produced when the chapter was built under Python 3.13.18 and not in your browser: [1, 2, 3, 128, 0]
nodes.definition: Bitcoin Core's header declares SIGHASH_ALL, NONE, SINGLE and ANYONECANPAY as 1, 2, 3 and 0x80 and adds SIGHASH_DEFAULT = 0 for taproot only.

nodes.label: Valid taproot hash types
nodes.body: BIP341 defines the signature message of taproot and lists exactly the hash types that are allowed: the default 0x00 (which is written by leaving the byte out) and the six combinations 0x01, 0x02, 0x03, 0x81, 0x82 and 0x83. The chapter's implementation of the BIP341 signature message is run on all 256 byte values and returns a digest for exactly those seven, ['0x0', '0x1', '0x2', '0x3', '0x81', '0x82', '0x83'], and nothing for the other 249. Bitcoin Core enforces the same rule and the regtest run in a later leaf shows what it says about an explicit zero byte (Wuille et al., 2020).
nodes.definition: A taproot signature may use only the hash types 0x00, 0x01, 0x02, 0x03, 0x81, 0x82 and 0x83, and every other byte value makes the signature invalid.

nodes.label: ANYPREVOUT values (BIP118)
nodes.body: The book mentions BIP118 as a proposal that would let a signature leave out the identity of the coin being spent, so that one signature can be reused for any coin with the same script, which is the feature that the eltoo design for the Lightning Network needs. The chapter reads the values from the saved BIP text, 64 (0x40) for SIGHASH_ANYPREVOUT and 192 (0xc0) for SIGHASH_ANYPREVOUTANYSCRIPT, and the BIP index at the pinned commit still lists it with the status Draft, so it is not part of the rules that any node enforces and Bitcoin Core does not list it among the BIPs it implements (Decker and Towns, 2017). This example reads bip-0118.mediawiki, a file saved with the chapter's evidence (the fetched sources, their test vectors or the record of Bitcoin Core 31.1.0's run), and a browser does not have it. Recorded output, produced when the chapter was built under Python 3.13.18 and not in your browser: [64, 192]
nodes.definition: The proposal BIP118 would add the flags SIGHASH_ANYPREVOUT = 0x40 and SIGHASH_ANYPREVOUTANYSCRIPT = 0xc0 to tapscript, and it is still only a draft.

nodes.label: The flag byte by hand
nodes.body: Bitcoin Core defines SIGHASH_ALL as 1, SIGHASH_NONE as 2, SIGHASH_SINGLE as 3 and SIGHASH_ANYONECANPAY as 0x80 (Bitcoin Core, 2026), and the book says that the modifier has the value 0x80 and is applied by bitwise OR, so SINGLE with the modifier is 0x83 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The example builds the byte from a base of 3 and a switch for the modifier, giving 131, which is 0x83, and then takes it apart again with a bit mask: the two lowest bits give back the base 3 and the top bit says whether ANYONECANPAY is set. The reader can change the base to 1 or 2 or switch the modifier off. It is like a light switch panel in which the low switches choose a mode and the top switch chooses whether other people may add inputs. A node reads the byte exactly this way when it checks which parts of a transaction a signature covers.
nodes.example: SINGLE with ANYONECANPAY is the byte 0x83
nodes.definition: The flag byte is the base value 1, 2 or 3 combined by bitwise OR with 0x80 for ANYONECANPAY, so 0x83 means SINGLE together with ANYONECANPAY.

io.code: base = 3; acp = 1; flag = base + 128 * acp; (flag, flag & 3, flag & 128 != 0)

nodes.label: What each flag commits to
nodes.body: This group measures what each flag commits to, by changing one field of a transaction at a time and by testing the signatures that Bitcoin Core made, and it shows the role of ANYONECANPAY (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.label: Matrix of commitments
nodes.body: The chapter finds what each flag commits to by experiment: it takes a transaction with three inputs and three outputs, computes the hash that input 1 signs, changes one field at a time and records whether the hash changed. The probes are, in order, the outpoint of another input, the sequence number of another input, the output with the same index, the other outputs, and the input's own sequence number. The results are 0x01 ALL [1,1,1,1,1]; 0x02 NONE [1,0,0,0,1]; 0x03 SINGLE [1,0,1,0,1]; 0x81 [0,0,1,1,1]; 0x82 [0,0,0,0,1]; 0x83 [0,0,1,0,1]. The book's table says ALL, NONE and SINGLE sign 'all inputs', which holds for the outpoints but not for the sequence numbers of the other inputs, which NONE and SINGLE leave out, as BIP143 also says (Lau and Wuille, 2016).
nodes.definition: A matrix of five probes shows what each flag commits to: changing a field that the flag covers changes the hash of the signed input, changing one it does not cover leaves it unchanged.

nodes.label: Survival of Core's signatures
nodes.body: The chapter asks Bitcoin Core 31.1, running on a private test network, to sign three-input segwit transactions with each flag, and then modifies a copy in two ways and verifies the first input's signature again with the chapter's own code: first the amount of the output with the same index as the input, then the amount of a different output. The answers, as [after the first change, after the second], are ALL [False, False], NONE [True, True], SINGLE [False, True], ALL|ANYONECANPAY [False, False], NONE|ANYONECANPAY [True, True] and SINGLE|ANYONECANPAY [False, True]. This confirms with independent software the claim of the book's table that SINGLE protects exactly the output at its own index, from one run of the node (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). This example reads core_regtest_record_v1_0_0.json, a file saved with the chapter's evidence (the fetched sources, their test vectors or the record of Bitcoin Core 31.1.0's run), and a browser does not have it. Recorded output, produced when the chapter was built under Python 3.13.18 and not in your browser: {'ALL': [False, False], 'NONE': [True, True], 'SINGLE': [False, True], 'ALL|ANYONECANPAY': [False, False], 'NONE|ANYONECANPAY': [True, True], 'SINGLE|ANYONECANPAY': [False, True]}
nodes.example: does Core's own signature survive a change
nodes.definition: Signatures made by Bitcoin Core 31.1 with each flag survive exactly the changes the flag allows: NONE survives any change of outputs and SINGLE only a change of a different output.

nodes.label: Effect of ANYONECANPAY
nodes.body: The ANYONECANPAY modifier lets anybody add inputs to a transaction after one input has been signed, which the book uses for crowdfunding: the signer commits to the outputs that pay the goal and leaves the inputs open (and the Bitcoin Wiki's assurance contract example describes the same). The chapter changes the outpoint of the third input in each of the transactions that Bitcoin Core signed and checks the first input's signature again: it survives only with the ANYONECANPAY combinations, {'ALL': False, 'NONE': False, 'SINGLE': False, 'ALL|ANYONECANPAY': True, 'NONE|ANYONECANPAY': True, 'SINGLE|ANYONECANPAY': True}. The Lightning Network's BOLT 3 specification uses SIGHASH_SINGLE|SIGHASH_ANYONECANPAY for the signatures of the second-stage transactions of channels with anchor outputs (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Lightning BOLTs, 2026) (Bitcoin Wiki, 2026). This example reads core_regtest_record_v1_0_0.json, a file saved with the chapter's evidence (the fetched sources, their test vectors or the record of Bitcoin Core 31.1.0's run), and a browser does not have it. Recorded output, produced when the chapter was built under Python 3.13.18 and not in your browser: {'ALL': False, 'NONE': False, 'SINGLE': False, 'ALL|ANYONECANPAY': True, 'NONE|ANYONECANPAY': True, 'SINGLE|ANYONECANPAY': True}
nodes.definition: With ANYONECANPAY a signature stays valid when the other inputs are replaced, which is what lets strangers add inputs to a crowdfunding transaction.

nodes.label: Flag bytes in Core's signatures
nodes.body: To see the flag as the network sees it, the chapter reads the last byte of the signature in each transaction that Bitcoin Core signed: 0x1 for ALL, 0x2 for NONE, 0x3 for SINGLE, 0x81, 0x82 and 0x83 for the ANYONECANPAY combinations. For taproot (bech32m) outputs, the signature has 65 bytes with the same flag byte for the six explicit flags, and 64 bytes with no flag byte when the default is used, in line with the book's statement that a 64-byte signature uses the default hash and one more byte makes it 65 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). This example reads core_regtest_record_v1_0_0.json, a file saved with the chapter's evidence (the fetched sources, their test vectors or the record of Bitcoin Core 31.1.0's run), and a browser does not have it. Recorded output, produced when the chapter was built under Python 3.13.18 and not in your browser: {'ALL': '0x1', 'NONE': '0x2', 'SINGLE': '0x3', 'ALL|ANYONECANPAY': '0x81', 'NONE|ANYONECANPAY': '0x82', 'SINGLE|ANYONECANPAY': '0x83', 'taproot ALL': [65, '0x1'], 'taproot NONE': [65, '0x2'], 'taproot SINGLE': [65, '0x3'], 'taproot ALL|ANYONECANPAY': [65, '0x81'], 'taproot NONE|ANYONECANPAY': [65, '0x82'], 'taproot SINGLE|ANYONECANPAY': [65, '0x83'], 'taproot DEFAULT': [64, None]}
nodes.example: the last byte of each signature
nodes.definition: The byte at the end of a signature Core made is the flag that was requested, and a taproot signature made with the default flag has 64 bytes and no flag byte.

nodes.label: Core's signatures verify
nodes.body: As an independent check of the chapter's code, Bitcoin Core 31.1 signed 25 transactions of three inputs on a private test network: for each of the four address types legacy, p2sh-segwit, bech32 and bech32m, one transaction per flag (six), plus the taproot default. The chapter's library, which implements the legacy algorithm, the BIP143 algorithm for segwit version 0 and the BIP341 algorithm for taproot, recomputes the digest of every one of the 75 inputs and verifies the signature: the result is (75, 75). One run of the node on 15 October 2026 is the evidence; a different run would give different signatures but the same count (Bitcoin Core, 2026). This example reads core_regtest_record_v1_0_0.json, a file saved with the chapter's evidence (the fetched sources, their test vectors or the record of Bitcoin Core 31.1.0's run), and a browser does not have it. Recorded output, produced when the chapter was built under Python 3.13.18 and not in your browser: (75, 75)
nodes.definition: Every one of the 75 signatures in the 25 transactions that Bitcoin Core 31.1 signed verifies with the chapter's own implementation of all four signature hash algorithms.

nodes.label: Known pitfalls of the flags
nodes.body: This group collects a flaw the book does not mention, the SIGHASH_SINGLE bug, how Bitcoin Core reacts to it, and the test vectors of Bitcoin Core that guard the legacy hash against such errors (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

nodes.label: The SIGHASH_SINGLE bug
nodes.body: SIGHASH_SINGLE signs the output that has the same position as the input, but nothing in the original code handled an input whose position was larger than the number of outputs: the function returned the 256-bit number one, 0100...00, as if it were the hash, and every transaction with such an input then has the same digest. Bitcoin Core's source marks the line with a comment about the bug and returns uint256::ONE; the chapter reproduces it and finds the digest equal to the byte string '01' followed by 31 zero bytes (True). The book's table does not mention this case, and the Bitcoin Wiki's page on the signature hash procedure documents it (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Bitcoin Wiki, 2026).
nodes.example: a hash equal to the number one
nodes.definition: In the legacy algorithm, SIGHASH_SINGLE on an input that has no output of the same index does not sign a hash of the transaction but the number one.

nodes.label: Core refuses the SINGLE bug
nodes.body: Bitcoin Core's signing code explains why it should not sign such an input: the signature would commit to no output at all, so it would stay valid if the output were swapped, which the comment calls a footgun, and it ends 'So don't produce it.' The code returns without a signature, and the regtest run confirms it: asked to sign with SINGLE a two-input transaction with one output, the node signs the first input and reports for the second 'Unable to sign input, invalid stack size (possibly missing key)', so 'complete' is False, whereas the same transaction with two outputs is signed completely (True). The pair is [False, True] (Bitcoin Core, 2026). This example reads core_regtest_record_v1_0_0.json, a file saved with the chapter's evidence (the fetched sources, their test vectors or the record of Bitcoin Core 31.1.0's run), and a browser does not have it. Recorded output, produced when the chapter was built under Python 3.13.18 and not in your browser: [False, True]
nodes.example: Bitcoin Core will not sign it
nodes.definition: Bitcoin Core 31.1 leaves such an input unsigned instead of creating the signature of the number one.

nodes.label: Core's sighash test vectors
nodes.body: Bitcoin Core keeps a data file, src/test/data/sighash.json, with 500 random transactions, scripts, input indices and hash types together with the signature hash that the node must compute. The chapter's implementation of the legacy algorithm reproduces the digest in every one of the 500 vectors, and the vectors contain 8 different hash-type bytes (including values that are not valid flags, which the old algorithm treated as ALL), so the result is (500, 500, 8). This is the independent check that the single-purpose code in the chapter computes what the network computes (Bitcoin Core, 2026). This example reads core_src_test_data_sighash.json, a file saved with the chapter's evidence (the fetched sources, their test vectors or the record of Bitcoin Core 31.1.0's run), and a browser does not have it. Recorded output, produced when the chapter was built under Python 3.13.18 and not in your browser: (500, 500, 8)
nodes.definition: The chapter's legacy signature hash agrees with Bitcoin Core's own test file for all 500 vectors, which cover eight kinds of hash types.

nodes.label: Inputs without an output
nodes.body: The book says that SINGLE signs the one output with the same index number as the signed input (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023), but a transaction can have more inputs than outputs, and for an input whose index has no matching output the legacy signature hash function returns the number one instead of a hash, a defect known as the SIGHASH_SINGLE bug, which the source of Bitcoin Core shows as a branch that returns the constant ONE when the input index is not below the number of outputs (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The example lists the inputs that run into it: with 3 inputs and 2 outputs the indexes are 0, 1 and 2, and only index 2 has no output, so the list is [2]; the reader can change the numbers and watch the list grow or vanish. It is like seating guests at numbered chairs where the third guest has no chair: the host's rule gives no answer, and the old software quietly answers with a fixed number that anyone can sign. Bitcoin Core refuses to sign in that case, as an earlier example of the chapter shows.
nodes.example: which inputs of 3 have no output to sign
nodes.definition: With SIGHASH_SINGLE an input whose index is not smaller than the number of outputs has no output to sign, which is the case that the legacy algorithm answers with the number one.

io.code: inputs = 3; outputs = 2; (inputs > outputs, [i for i in range(inputs) if i >= outputs])

nodes.label: Schnorr signatures
nodes.body: Schnorr signatures, introduced to Bitcoin by the taproot soft fork of November 2021 as BIP340, are the newer of the two signature algorithms of the chapter and the one whose mathematics is simplest: a three-move proof of knowledge of a private key, turned into a signature by replacing the verifier's challenge with a hash. This branch walks from the toy protocol with ordinary integers to the 64-byte format of BIP340, then to the consequences of the algebra that the book highlights, namely the linearity that allows batch verification, scriptless multisignatures that look like one signature, and threshold signatures built on Shamir's secret sharing. Each step is computed, and the format is checked against the 19 official test vectors (Wuille et al., 2020).

nodes.label: From identity proof to signature
nodes.body: This group builds the schnorr signature step by step: the toy protocol with integers, the identification round with points on the curve, what goes wrong if the order of the moves is changed, and the Fiat-Shamir step that makes it a signature (Fiat and Shamir, 1986).

nodes.label: The toy protocol with integers
nodes.body: The book teaches the schnorr protocol first with whole numbers in place of curve points. Let the private key be x = 3 and the generator G = 5, so the public key is xG = 15; the nonce is k = 7, so the public nonce is kG = 35; the challenge is e = 11, and the response is s = k + e x = 40. The verifier checks that sG = 200 equals kG + e(xG) = 35 + 165 = 200, which holds. The chapter's script returns [15, 35, 40, 200, 165, True, 3] and the last number shows the weakness of the toy: dividing the public key 15 by G = 5 gives back the private key 3, which is exactly why the real protocol uses points on an elliptic curve, where this division is the discrete logarithm problem that nobody can solve (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
nodes.example: x = 3, G = 5, k = 7, e = 11 with plain integers
nodes.definition: With ordinary integers the identification protocol works, s = k + e x satisfies s G = k G + e (x G), but anybody can divide by G, so the private key is exposed.

nodes.label: One round of the identity proof
nodes.body: The interactive protocol has three moves: the prover sends a commitment, the public nonce kG; the verifier answers with a random challenge e; the prover replies with s = k + e x modulo n. The verifier then checks that s times G equals kG plus e times the public key X. The chapter runs one round on secp256k1 with a test private key, a test nonce and a challenge made from a hash, and the check returns True. The nonce is what hides the key: s alone is the key mixed with a random number, so it reveals nothing, but with a different challenge and the same nonce it would, which is why a nonce must be used once (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
nodes.definition: On the real curve the same three moves (commitment kG, challenge e, response s) are checked by one equation, sG = kG + eX, and it holds.

nodes.label: A wrong response
nodes.body: The soundness of the protocol is that only a prover who knows x can produce a response that satisfies the equation for a challenge that was chosen after the commitment. The chapter takes the correct response, adds one, and checks the equation again: the answer is False. A cheating prover who guesses a response must guess a 256-bit number, which has a probability of about 1 in 2 to the 256, and a prover who could answer two different challenges for one commitment could compute the private key from the two answers, which is what makes the proof convincing (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
nodes.definition: If the response s is changed by even one unit, the verification equation no longer holds, so a prover without the private key cannot answer.

nodes.label: Order of commitment and challenge
nodes.body: The order of the moves matters. If a cheater knows the challenge e in advance, they can pick any response s, compute the commitment as sG minus eX, and the check passes without the private key; the chapter does this with a test key and the check returns True. The book states the consequence: the nonce commitment must be fixed before the challenge is revealed, so in the signature version the challenge has to come from something the signer cannot choose after the fact, which is where the hash function enters (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
nodes.definition: A prover who learns the challenge before committing can pass without the private key, which is why the commitment must come first.

nodes.label: The Fiat-Shamir signature
nodes.body: A signature cannot wait for a verifier to answer, so the challenge is computed as e = hash(kG, xG, m), where m is the message: the signer commits to the nonce, derives the challenge from the hash, and responds. Fiat and Shamir described this transformation in 1986 and Schnorr applied it to his identification scheme. The chapter's simplified signature verifies for its message (True) and fails for a different message (False), the list [True, False]. Pointcheval and Stern (2000) give security arguments for digital signatures in the random oracle model, in which the hash function is treated as an ideal random object. Because the message is inside the hash, the signature is bound to it, and because the public key is inside the hash too, the signature is bound to the key, which is the key-prefixing property of the next leaf (Fiat and Shamir, 1986) (Schnorr, 1991).
nodes.example: a hash in place of the verifier
nodes.definition: The Fiat-Shamir transform replaces the verifier's random challenge by a hash of the commitment, the key and the message, which turns the interactive proof into a signature on that message.

nodes.label: An identity round with small numbers
nodes.body: In the book's identification protocol Alice commits to a nonce point kG, Bob answers with a challenge e, Alice replies with s = k + e x, and Bob accepts when sG equals kG plus e times xG, which he can compute without knowing x or k (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The example plays one round in the stand-in group of integers modulo 101 with the private key 12, the nonce 6 and the challenge 9: the response is s = 13, and both sides of the check give the same number, so the answer is True. The reader can change the key, the nonce or the challenge, and the check keeps holding, because the equation is an identity; to see it fail, change s by one after it is computed. It is like a secret handshake in which only the true partner can produce the matching grip. As in the other toy examples, the real protocol runs on secp256k1, where the division that would reveal x is impossible.
nodes.example: one round of the identity proof with integers modulo 101
nodes.definition: With the response s = k + e x, the verifier's check s g = r + e X holds, and with a different response it would fail.

io.code: n = 101; g = 7; x = 12; k = 6; e = 9; big_x = x * g % n; big_r = k * g % n; s = (k + e * x) % n; (s, s * g % n == (big_r + e * big_x) % n)

nodes.label: The BIP340 format
nodes.body: This group covers the details that make the algorithm a standard: the test vectors, the 64-byte and 65-byte forms, the x-only keys, the tagged hashes, the default nonce and the key prefixing (Wuille et al., 2020).

nodes.label: BIP340 test vectors
nodes.body: BIP340 is the specification of the schnorr signature that Bitcoin uses in taproot, and its authors publish a table of test vectors with secret key, public key, auxiliary random data, message, signature and the expected verification result. The chapter's implementation gives the expected verification result for all 19 rows, including the invalid ones with wrong keys and out-of-range values, and for the 8 rows that include a secret key it also reproduces the public key and the exact signature. The result is [19, 19, 8, 8], which is the best evidence that the code follows the standard and not just the book's simplified protocol (Wuille et al., 2020). This example reads bip-0340_test-vectors.csv, a file saved with the chapter's evidence (the fetched sources, their test vectors or the record of Bitcoin Core 31.1.0's run), and a browser does not have it. Recorded output, produced when the chapter was built under Python 3.13.18 and not in your browser: [19, 19, 8, 8]
nodes.definition: The chapter's BIP340 implementation matches all 19 vectors of the BIP, verifying 19 and reproducing the signature of each of the 8 vectors that give a secret key.

nodes.label: Schnorr signature sizes
nodes.body: The book explains the serialization: the signature is the x coordinate of kG (32 bytes) followed by the scalar s (32 bytes), 64 bytes in all and always the same length, unlike the variable length of ECDSA signatures. In a taproot input a 64-byte signature means the default hash type and a 65-byte signature carries an explicit hash type as its last byte. The chapter signs with the default and with an explicit flag and gets [(64, True), (65, True)], each size with a signature that verifies (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Wuille et al., 2020).
nodes.definition: A BIP340 signature has 64 bytes, the 32-byte x coordinate of the nonce point followed by the 32-byte scalar s, and in taproot one more byte may name a hash type.

nodes.label: X-only public keys
nodes.body: Bitcoin's compressed public keys have 33 bytes: a prefix for the parity of y and the 32-byte x. BIP340 saves the prefix by agreeing that the y coordinate is always the even one, so a public key is 32 bytes. If the real point has an odd y, the signer replaces the private key d by n minus d, whose point has the same x and an even y. The chapter shows for a test key that the x-only key has 32 bytes, that the parity of the point's y is 0 in this case, and that d and n minus d give the same x-only key, the list [32, 0, True]. The book simplifies this detail away when it says only the x coordinate of kG is included (Wuille et al., 2020).
nodes.definition: A BIP340 public key is only the 32-byte x coordinate, and the signer negates the private key when the point's y coordinate is odd so that a key and its negative give the same public key.

nodes.label: Tagged hashes
nodes.body: The challenge e of BIP340 is not the plain SHA-256 of the data but a tagged hash, defined as SHA256(SHA256(tag) || SHA256(tag) || data) with the tag 'BIP0340/challenge'. The prefix is 64 bytes long, exactly one block of SHA-256, so an implementation can precompute the state after the prefix. Because every use of schnorr in Bitcoin has its own tag, a hash made for one purpose cannot be reused as a hash for another. The chapter's check confirms the length 64 for the prefix and that the tagged hash of a test input differs from the plain hash, the list [64, True] (Wuille et al., 2020).
nodes.definition: BIP340 hashes with a tag: the hash of the tag is computed once and put twice in front of the data, so that hashes made for different purposes cannot be confused.

nodes.label: The default BIP340 nonce
nodes.body: The book says BIP340 recommends a default algorithm for the nonce. It hashes the private key together with fresh auxiliary random data, hashes the result with the public key and the message to get k, and so the nonce depends on the message and the secret even if the auxiliary data is poor. The chapter signs the same message twice with the default (all-zero) auxiliary data and gets the same signature (True), signs once with other auxiliary data and gets a different one (True), and finds that the different signature also verifies (True): [True, True, True] (Wuille et al., 2020).
nodes.definition: The default BIP340 signing function derives its nonce from the key, the message and auxiliary data, so with the same inputs it gives the same signature and with other auxiliary data another one.

nodes.label: Key prefixing
nodes.body: The book explains that BIP340 commits to the public key in the challenge, hash(kG, xG, m), and the reason is practical. If the challenge were only hash(kG, m), then from a valid signature (kG, s) for the key P anybody could build, using public data only, a valid signature for the key P + aG, which is the key that unhardened BIP32 derivation would produce for the tweak a. The chapter implements both variants: without the key in the hash the forged signature verifies (True), with the key in the hash it fails (False), the list [True, False] (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Wuille, 2012).
nodes.example: hash(R, P, m) against hash(R, m)
nodes.definition: Including the public key in the challenge stops an attacker who knows a signature for one key from deriving a signature for a related key such as a BIP32 child key.

nodes.label: Bytes saved by schnorr
nodes.body: BIP340 compares keeping one bit of the Y coordinate, which would give 33-byte public keys and 65-byte signatures, with encoding only the X coordinate, which gives the 32-byte public keys and 64-byte signatures that it chooses (Wuille et al., 2020), while the book's ECDSA sample takes 72 bytes with its hash type (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) and a compressed key takes 33. The example subtracts the two totals, 105 against 96 bytes, to get 9 bytes for each input, multiplies by the number of inputs, and divides by 4 because witness bytes count one weight unit each and four weight units make one virtual byte, giving 6.75 virtual bytes saved for 3 inputs; the reader can change the number of inputs or the size of the ECDSA signature. It is like swapping a long address label for a short one on every parcel of a delivery. The saving is small for one input and grows with the count, and a real ECDSA signature may be 70 to 72 bytes.
nodes.example: 9 bytes saved for each input of 3
nodes.definition: A schnorr signature of 64 bytes with a 32-byte key replaces an ECDSA signature of 72 bytes with a 33-byte key, which saves 9 bytes of witness for each input and 27 for 3 inputs.

io.code: inputs = 3; ecdsa = 72; schnorr = 64; per = (ecdsa + 33) - (schnorr + 32); (per, per * inputs, per * inputs / 4)

nodes.label: The tag prefix fills a block
nodes.body: BIP340 includes the tag in a hash by prefixing the data with SHA256(tag) twice, and it explains that this is a 64-byte context-specific constant and that the block size of SHA-256 is also 64 bytes, so optimized implementations can start from a precomputed state (Wuille et al., 2020). The example hashes the tag BIP0340/challenge, the one used for the challenge of a signature, repeats the 32-byte result the chosen number of times, and tests whether the length is a whole number of 64-byte blocks: with 2 repetitions the length is 64 and the answer is True, and with 3 it is 96 and the answer is False, which the reader can try. It is like a stamp that always fills exactly one page of a notebook, so that the page can be stamped in advance. The prefix also separates the hashes of different purposes, so a challenge hash can never be mistaken for another kind of hash.
nodes.example: two hashes of the tag fill one 64-byte hash block
nodes.definition: BIP340 prefixes the data with the hash of the tag twice, which is 64 bytes and exactly one block of SHA-256, so an implementation can precompute it.

io.code: import hashlib; reps = 2; h = hashlib.sha256(b'BIP0340/challenge').digest(); (len(h * reps), len(h * reps) % 64 == 0)

nodes.label: Aggregating keys and signatures
nodes.body: This group covers what linearity allows: batch verification, the scriptless multisignature, the key cancellation attack against it and MuSig2, the standard that defends against it (Nick et al., 2022).

nodes.label: Linearity
nodes.body: A function is linear if it satisfies additivity, f(x + y) = f(x) + f(y), and homogeneity, f(a x) = a f(x). The map from a private key v to the point vG is linear, because it is repeated addition of G. The chapter checks both properties for chosen numbers, [True, True]. The schnorr response s = k + e x is also linear in the private key and the nonce, so the sums of the signers' keys, nonces and responses are the key, the nonce and the response of the combined signer, which is the property the next leaves use for multisignatures and batch verification (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
nodes.example: f(x + y + z) = f(x) + f(y) + f(z)
nodes.definition: Multiplying the generator by a scalar is additive and homogeneous, which is why signatures and keys of several signers can be added.

nodes.label: Batch verification
nodes.body: Verification of one schnorr signature checks sG = R + eP. Multiplying the equation of each signature by a random weight and adding them gives a single equation that is true if all signatures are valid and, with overwhelming probability, false if any is not; the weights stop a forger from arranging that two bad signatures cancel. The chapter takes the 9 valid signatures of the BIP340 test vectors, finds that the combined equation holds (True), swaps one signature for another and finds that it fails (False): [9, True, False]. The book's statement that batch verification takes about half the time of verifying one by one is not reproduced here, because the library's README lists no batch API (Wuille et al., 2020) (Bitcoin Core, 2026). This example reads bip-0340_test-vectors.csv, a file saved with the chapter's evidence (the fetched sources, their test vectors or the record of Bitcoin Core 31.1.0's run), and a browser does not have it. Recorded output, produced when the chapter was built under Python 3.13.18 and not in your browser: [9, True, False]
nodes.definition: Because the equation is linear, many signatures can be verified together as one random combination of their equations, and one bad signature in the batch makes the combined check fail.

nodes.label: Naive scriptless multisignature
nodes.body: In a scriptless multisignature the signers add their public keys into one aggregate key, add their nonces into one aggregate nonce, compute one challenge from the aggregates, and each returns a response; the sum of the responses is the signature. The chapter does this for two test signers and the combined signature verifies against the sum of their keys (True), and the sum is indeed the sum of the two public points (True): [True, True]. On the blockchain this is a single key and a single 64-byte signature, which is both smaller than a script multisignature and indistinguishable from a single-signer payment (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
nodes.example: two keys added, two responses added
nodes.definition: Two signers can add their public keys and their signatures into one key and one signature that verifies, which looks like the signature of a single person.

nodes.label: Key cancellation attack
nodes.body: The naive protocol is unsafe. If Bob waits to see Alice's public key yG and then publishes the key zG minus yG, the aggregate is yG + (zG - yG) = zG, a key whose private key z only Bob knows, so Bob can sign alone for both. The book calls this the key cancellation attack and says that safe protocols must prevent it. The chapter performs it on the naive aggregation: the aggregate equals zG (True) and the signature Bob makes alone verifies against it (True): [True, True]. This is a rogue-key attack, and the MuSig family was designed against it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Maxwell et al., 2019).
nodes.definition: In the naive protocol the last signer to publish a key can choose it as their key minus the sum of the others, and then control the aggregate alone.

nodes.label: MuSig2 key aggregation
nodes.body: MuSig2 (Nick et al., 2021), standardized as BIP327 with the status Deployed, fixes the naive protocol by multiplying each signer's key by a coefficient that is a hash of the whole list of keys and that signer's own key, so that no one can choose a key as a function of the others' after seeing them. The chapter implements the BIP327 key aggregation algorithm and checks it against the BIP's own key aggregation test vectors, valid and invalid: the result is [4, 4], four checked and four matching. It is key aggregation only; the two-round signing is not implemented here (Nick et al., 2022) (Nick et al., 2021). This example reads bip-0327_key_agg_vectors.json, a file saved with the chapter's evidence (the fetched sources, their test vectors or the record of Bitcoin Core 31.1.0's run), and a browser does not have it. Recorded output, produced when the chapter was built under Python 3.13.18 and not in your browser: [4, 4]
nodes.definition: The MuSig2 key aggregation of BIP327 weights each key by a coefficient derived from all the keys, and the chapter's implementation reproduces the BIP's test vectors.

nodes.label: MuSig2 against key cancellation
nodes.body: The chapter repeats the attack of the naive protocol against the aggregation of BIP327: Bob publishes zG minus yG after seeing Alice's key yG and the aggregate key is computed with the coefficients. The aggregate is not zG, so Bob's private key z does not control it, and the answer to the question 'is the aggregate Bob's key' is False. This is the property that the key cancellation attack breaks in the naive protocol and the reason Bitcoin Core can support the musig() descriptor for aggregated keys (Nick et al., 2022) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).
nodes.example: the same attack against MuSig2 keys
nodes.definition: With BIP327's coefficients the aggregate of Alice's key and Bob's cancelling key is no longer Bob's key, so Bob cannot sign alone.

nodes.label: Key cancellation with small numbers
nodes.body: The book describes the key cancellation attack: Bob generates his public key as zG minus yG, so that when the two keys are combined, yG plus zG minus yG, the positive and negative terms cancel and the combined key represents only Bob's private key z, after which he can sign without Alice (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The example uses the integers modulo 101: Alice's key is 12 times 7, Bob's announced key is 5 times 7 minus Alice's, and their sum is 35, which equals 5 times 7, so Bob who knows 5 controls the aggregate. The reader can change Bob's number and the check stays True, which is the point: whatever Bob picks, he can cancel Alice. It is like two people signing a joint cheque where one of them quietly swaps the account for his own. MuSig2 prevents this by weighting each key with a coefficient that depends on all the keys, as the standard states (Nick et al., 2022).
nodes.example: Bob's key hides Alice's key and he signs alone
nodes.definition: If Bob announces his key as m g minus Alice's key, the sum of the two keys is m g, a key that Bob alone controls.

io.code: n = 101; g = 7; a = 12; m = 5; xa = a * g % n; xm = (m * g - xa) % n; agg = (xa + xm) % n; (agg == m * g % n, agg)

nodes.label: Threshold signatures from secret sharing
nodes.body: This group covers the threshold signatures that the book builds from Shamir's secret sharing, any two of three signers, why one share reveals nothing and the manipulation attack that the book warns about (Shamir, 1979).

nodes.label: Shamir secret sharing
nodes.body: A threshold signature lets a subset of the key holders sign, for example any 2 of 3. The book builds it from the secret sharing of Shamir (1979): to share a secret d among three people so that any two can rebuild it, choose a random line f(x) = d + cx, give the person i the share f(i), and recover d from any two points by interpolating the line back to x = 0. In the chapter's scriptless protocol each of Alice, Bob and Carol shares their partial private key this way; Alice and Bob rebuild Carol's key from the two shares they hold, and together sign a message so that the signature verifies for the sum of the three keys. The three answers are [rebuilt key equals Carol's, signature verifies, aggregate key is the sum] = [True, True, True] (Shamir, 1979) (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
nodes.definition: Shamir's secret sharing hides a secret as the constant term of a polynomial and gives each holder one point, so that any two of three points rebuild the secret by interpolation.

nodes.label: Any two of three shares
nodes.body: The chapter shares the number 31337 with a line, so that the three shares are three points of it, and rebuilds the secret from each of the three pairs of shares: the answer is 31337 each time, [31337, 31337, 31337]. Interpolation is done modulo n, the order of the curve, which is where the scalars of the signature live, and any k shares of a polynomial of degree k - 1 determine it uniquely, which is the theorem of Shamir's paper: knowledge of any k or more pieces makes the secret easily computable (Shamir, 1979).
nodes.definition: Any two of the three shares give the same secret, here the number 31337.

nodes.label: Secrecy of a single share
nodes.body: The other half of the guarantee is secrecy: fewer than the threshold of shares give no information. The chapter takes one share (a point), picks a different secret, computes the slope that would make that secret's line pass through the same point, and finds that the share is the same, so the one point is consistent with every possible secret, and the answer is True. A holder of one share therefore learns nothing about the key, and a thief who steals one share cannot sign (Shamir, 1979) (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
nodes.example: one share is consistent with every secret
nodes.definition: A single share of a 2-of-3 sharing reveals nothing, because for any other secret there is a line through the same point.

nodes.label: Manipulation attack
nodes.body: The book warns that its scriptless threshold protocol has a flaw, which it calls manipulation: Bob tells Alice that Carol is unavailable, so Alice and Bob rebuild Carol's partial key from the shares they hold; then he tells Carol that Alice is unavailable, so Bob and Carol rebuild Alice's partial key. Bob now holds all three keys and can sign alone. The chapter performs it and gets [Carol's key rebuilt, Alice's key rebuilt, Bob holds the sum of all three] = [True, True, True]. The book says no scriptless threshold protocol had been proposed as a BIP; this is the kind of flaw that a standard protocol must remove (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
nodes.example: Bob tells each that the other is away
nodes.definition: In the book's simple threshold protocol a dishonest member can obtain the others' partial keys by claiming in turn that each of the others is unavailable.

nodes.label: Shamir sharing modulo 101
nodes.body: Shamir's scheme hides a secret D as the value of a random polynomial at zero, over a prime larger than both the secret and the number of holders, and any k pieces recover it while k - 1 or fewer leave it completely undetermined (Shamir, 1979); the book calls the basic idea secret sharing and uses it for threshold signatures (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The example uses the line 7 + 3 x modulo 101, so the three holders receive 10, 13 and 16; holders 1 and 3 compute the slope as the difference of their values divided by the difference of their positions, which is 3, and subtract it from the first share to get back 7. The reader can change the secret, the slope or the prime. It is like a map torn into three pieces along lines so that any two overlap enough to show the treasure. The prime 101 is only for teaching, since a real secret needs a prime far larger than itself.
nodes.example: secret 7 shared as a line modulo 101, any two shares return it
nodes.definition: A secret of 7 and a slope of 3 give the shares 10, 13 and 16 at x = 1, 2 and 3 modulo 101, and the first and third shares return the secret 7.

nodes.label: ECDSA signatures
nodes.body: ECDSA is the signature algorithm that Bitcoin used from its first release and that it still uses for every output that is not a taproot output. This branch gives its equations, shows the malleability that results from its form, explains the DER serialization of the book's example (itself a real signature from the blockchain) and separates what the network enforces as consensus from what a node only relays as policy. The statements are tested on the book's own sample, on signatures made by the chapter's library and on the answers of Bitcoin Core 31.1 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Wuille, 2015).

nodes.label: The ECDSA equations
nodes.body: This group gives the ECDSA equations, the malleability that follows from them and the low-S rule that removes it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.label: ECDSA formulas
nodes.body: ECDSA, the Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm, produces a signature of two numbers, R and s. The signer picks a private nonce k, computes the public nonce K = kG, and takes R as the x coordinate of K; then s = k^-1 (hash(m) + x R) modulo n, where x is the private key and k^-1 is the modular inverse. The verifier computes the point u1 G + u2 X with u1 = hash(m) / s and u2 = R / s, all modulo n, and accepts when its x coordinate equals R. Unlike schnorr, the equation is not linear in the nonce and key, which is why the clean aggregation of the previous section is not available. The chapter implements the formulas exactly as the book gives them: the signature verifies (True), fails for another message hash (False) and its R equals the x coordinate of kG (True), the list [True, False, True] (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (NIST, 2023).
nodes.example: s = k^-1 (hash(m) + x R) mod n
nodes.definition: ECDSA signs with a random nonce k, takes R as the x coordinate of kG and computes s = k^-1 (hash + x R) modulo n; the verifier recomputes R from s, the hash and the public key.

nodes.label: Signature malleability
nodes.body: A signature scheme is malleable if someone other than the signer can turn a valid signature into a different valid signature for the same message. ECDSA is: if (R, s) verifies, then (R, n - s) verifies too, because replacing s by its negative flips the sign of the point u1 G + u2 X but leaves its x coordinate unchanged. The chapter's check gives [True, True, True]: the original verifies, the negated one verifies, and exactly one of the two is the 'low' value at most n/2. Before segwit a changed signature changed the transaction identifier, because the signature was inside the transaction that is hashed to the txid, which BIP146 describes as the ability of any relay node to transform the signature without the key, and BIP146 made the high form non-standard (Lau and Wuille, 2016) (Wuille et al., 2020).
nodes.definition: For every valid ECDSA signature (R, s) the pair (R, n - s) is also valid for the same message, so a third party can change a signature without knowing the key.

nodes.label: The low-S rule
nodes.body: To remove the malleability, a signer chooses between s and n - s the one that is at most n/2, which is called the low-S rule. Bitcoin Core's verification function normalizes the received s and its policy rejects the high form. The chapter's signing function follows the rule: of 200 signatures it makes for 200 different keys and messages, all pass the strict DER check ported from Core (True), all have a low s (True), and their DER lengths are 70 and 71 bytes without the hash type byte, [True, True, [70, 71]], the two lengths that depend on whether the random-looking R happens to have its top bit set (Bitcoin Core, 2026).
nodes.example: always the smaller of s and n - s
nodes.definition: The chapter's signer always returns the low s, so every signature it makes passes the strict DER and low-S rules, with lengths 70 or 71 bytes.

nodes.label: ECDSA with small numbers
nodes.body: The book gives the signing equation of ECDSA as s = k^-1 (Hash(m) + x times R), where k is the private nonce, R is the x coordinate of the public nonce and x is the private key (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). In the example the private key d is 17, the nonce k is 29, the digest z is 11 and the group is the integers modulo 101 with the generator 7, so the public key is q = 17 times 7 modulo 101, the nonce point is r = 29 times 7 modulo 101 and the signature value is s = 95; the verifier computes w as the inverse of s, forms z times w times g plus r times w times q, and gets back r, which is the answer True. It is like a lock and key cut from one blank: the verifier never sees d or k, yet the numbers fit only when both were used together. Because ordinary multiplication stands in for the multiplication of curve points, the algebra is exact but the secrecy is not, since anyone can divide; a real curve has no such division, and that is where the security lies.
nodes.example: sign and verify with ECDSA's equations modulo 101
nodes.definition: With a stand-in group of integers modulo 101, the ECDSA equation s = k^-1 (z + r d) gives a signature that the verifier's combination of z/s and r/s accepts.

nodes.label: The other valid S
nodes.body: ECDSA signatures are malleable because the verification equation treats s and its negative modulo the group order n alike, so a third party can turn a valid signature into another valid one without knowing any key (Wuille et al., 2020). BIP146 answers this for scripts by requiring that the S value be at most the curve order divided by 2, the lower half of its range (Lau and Wuille, 2016). With the stand-in order 101 and s equal to 30, the partner value is 71, and the test s at most n divided by 2 is True for 30 and False for 71, so exactly one of the pair passes; the reader can change s to see that the halves swap at 51. It is like a coin with two faces that both name the same owner: the rule only fixes which face a signature must show. The real order has 256 bits, but the rule is the same comparison, and in Bitcoin Core it is a relay policy, which the next examples of the chapter separate from consensus.
nodes.example: s and n - s both verify, only one is low
nodes.definition: If s is a valid ECDSA value then n - s is valid too, and exactly one of the two lies in the lower half of the range that BIP146 asks for.

nodes.label: DER serialization
nodes.body: This group takes the book's DER example apart, shows that it is a real signature from December 2013, verifies it, and notes its high R value (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.label: Layout of a DER signature
nodes.body: DER, the Distinguished Encoding Rules, is a standard way to write structured data as bytes, and Bitcoin used it for ECDSA signatures from the start. The book's sample is 3045 0221 00884d...81 0220 4b9f...13 01. The elements, as the chapter's parser finds, are: 0x30 (a sequence follows), 0x45 (its length, 69 bytes), 0x02 (an integer follows), 0x21 (length 33), the integer R with a leading 0x00 because its top bit is set and DER integers are signed, 0x02, 0x20 (length 32), the integer S, and the Bitcoin hash type byte 0x01, nine elements in all. The whole is 72 bytes, the string passes Bitcoin Core's strict DER check, and the result [72, 69, '30', '45', '21', '20', '01', 9, True] confirms the book (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Wuille, 2015).
nodes.definition: A DER-encoded ECDSA signature is a sequence of two integers, tagged 0x30, with a length byte, followed in Bitcoin by the hash type byte; the book's sample has nine elements.

nodes.label: The book's sample on the chain
nodes.body: The long hexadecimal string that the book dissects was not made up for the book: the chapter finds it, byte for byte, in the saved record of the transaction 0627052b6f28912f2703066a912ea577f2ce4da4caa5a5fbd8a57286c345c2f2 from the mempool.space block explorer. The record says the transaction is in block 277,316 with the block time 1388185914, that is 2013-12-27 23:11:54 UTC. The result [True, 277316, 1388185914] shows that the signature is in the input's scriptSig (the unlocking script of chapter 7) and where it is on the chain (Mempool Space, 2026) (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). This example reads mainnet_tx_0627052b.json, a file saved with the chapter's evidence (the fetched sources, their test vectors or the record of Bitcoin Core 31.1.0's run), and a browser does not have it. Recorded output, produced when the chapter was built under Python 3.13.18 and not in your browser: [True, 277316, 1388185914]
nodes.definition: The signature in the book's DER section is the real signature of a main-chain transaction mined on 27 December 2013.

nodes.label: The sample verifies
nodes.body: Because the sample is a real signature, the chapter checks it as a node would: it takes the input's 65-byte uncompressed public key, rebuilds the legacy signature hash of the transaction with the previous output's script and the hash type 01 (SIGHASH_ALL), and verifies. The result is [65, 1, True, False, 72]: the key has 65 bytes, the hash type is 1, the signature verifies, it does not verify when the hash is computed with hash type 2 (NONE), and the signature with its flag byte is 72 bytes. This shows the machinery of the chapter on a live example from the chain (Mempool Space, 2026) (Bitcoin Core, 2026). This example reads mainnet_tx_0627052b.json, a file saved with the chapter's evidence (the fetched sources, their test vectors or the record of Bitcoin Core 31.1.0's run), and a browser does not have it. Recorded output, produced when the chapter was built under Python 3.13.18 and not in your browser: [65, 1, True, False, 72]
nodes.example: the signature, the key and the transaction agree
nodes.definition: The book's sample verifies against the legacy signature hash of its transaction and the 65-byte public key in the same input, and fails if the hash type is changed.

nodes.label: The sample's high R
nodes.body: In DER an integer is signed, so a 256-bit number whose top bit is set needs a leading 0x00 byte to stay positive, which is why the sample's R takes 33 bytes. The chapter finds for the sample that s is at most n/2 (True), that R is at least 2 to the 255 (True) and that R has 64 hexadecimal digits, that is 32 bytes without the padding. About half of all random R values have the top bit set, so about half of the older Bitcoin signatures were 72 bytes with the flag, and Bitcoin Core now avoids this by trying nonces until R is small, as the randomness section below shows (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).
nodes.definition: The sample's R has its top bit set, which costs a padding zero and one extra byte, while its s is the low form.

nodes.label: The padding zero of DER
nodes.body: The book prints a real signature, 3045022100884d..., and lists its nine elements: the byte 0x30 for a sequence, the length 0x45 of 69 bytes, then the integer R with its tag 0x02 and its length 0x21 of 33 bytes, and the integer S with its tag and its length of 32 bytes (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The first byte of R is 0x88, which is 136; because DER reads integers as signed, any first byte of 128 or more would be read as negative, so one zero byte is put in front, and that is why R takes 33 bytes and not 32. The example adds the pieces, 2 + 32 + 1 + 2 + 32 = 69 bytes of body, 71 bytes with the two header bytes and 72 with the hash type byte, and the reader can change the first byte of R to see the padding disappear. It is like a form with a sign box that must be ticked whenever the top digit is large. The strict form of this encoding is a consensus rule since BIP66 (Wuille, 2015).
nodes.example: a 33-byte R makes a 71-byte DER body
nodes.definition: A DER integer is signed, so an R whose first byte is 0x88 or higher needs a leading zero byte, which makes the book's signature 71 bytes before the hash type byte and 72 with it.

io.code: rtop = 136; rlen = 32; slen = 32; pad = int(rtop >= 128); body = 2 + rlen + pad + 2 + slen; (pad, body + 2, body + 3)

nodes.label: Consensus rules and relay policy
nodes.body: This group separates what Bitcoin Core refuses to relay from what makes a block invalid, using the verdicts of the node on altered signatures and the limit on legacy signature operations (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

nodes.label: Core's policy verdicts
nodes.body: A node applies stricter rules to the transactions it relays than the consensus rules that decide whether a block is valid. The chapter has Bitcoin Core 31.1 test four versions of the same spend, made with the chapter's own key on the private test network: the ordinary low-S signature is allowed; the high-S version is refused with 'Non-canonical signature: S value is unnecessarily high'; a version with a non-minimal DER padding is refused with 'Non-canonical DER signature'; and a signature of another message is refused because, for a failed check, the signature must be the empty value ('Signature must be zero for failed CHECK(MULTI)SIG operation'). Each verdict is read from the node's testmempoolaccept answer (Bitcoin Core, 2026). This example reads core_regtest_record_v1_0_0.json, a file saved with the chapter's evidence (the fetched sources, their test vectors or the record of Bitcoin Core 31.1.0's run), and a browser does not have it. Recorded output, produced when the chapter was built under Python 3.13.18 and not in your browser: {'valid_low_s': [True, None], 'high_s': [False, 'mempool-script-verify-flag-failed (Non-canonical signature: S value is unnecessarily high)'], 'non_minimal_der': [False, 'mempool-script-verify-flag-failed (Non-canonical DER signature)'], 'signed_other_message': [False, 'mempool-script-verify-flag-failed (Signature must be zero for failed CHECK(MULTI)SIG operation)']}
nodes.definition: Bitcoin Core 31.1 accepts a normal signature into its mempool and rejects a high-S signature, a non-minimal DER encoding and a signature of another message with a specific error each.

nodes.label: Strict DER is consensus
nodes.body: The difference between policy and consensus can be tested by asking the node to put a transaction directly into a block, which skips the relay rules. In the regtest run the transaction with the high-S signature was accepted in a block (True), the one with a non-DER signature was not (False), and the error of the second contains 'Non-canonical DER signature' (True): [True, False, True]. The second rule is a consensus rule since BIP66 was activated by a soft fork in July 2015, when its 95 percent threshold was reached on 4 July, and Pieter Wuille later disclosed (28 July 2015) that a specially crafted transaction could have forked the blockchain between nodes with different signature parsers until BIP66 made it invalid (Wuille, 2015); the first is a relay rule only. The book, which does not separate them, is right that both kinds of signature are 'wrong' but wrong in different ways (Wuille, 2015) (Lau and Wuille, 2016). This example reads core_regtest_record_v1_0_0.json, a file saved with the chapter's evidence (the fetched sources, their test vectors or the record of Bitcoin Core 31.1.0's run), and a browser does not have it. Recorded output, produced when the chapter was built under Python 3.13.18 and not in your browser: [True, False, True]
nodes.example: mined in a block or not
nodes.definition: A high-S signature is valid in a block, because low-S is only policy, while a signature that is not strict DER makes the block invalid, because strict DER is a consensus rule.

nodes.label: Policy flags
nodes.body: In Bitcoin Core, the extra checks that a standard transaction must pass are written as script verification flags in src/policy/policy.h. The chapter reads the saved copy and finds all four named flags in it: SCRIPT_VERIFY_LOW_S (the smaller of s and n - s), SCRIPT_VERIFY_NULLFAIL (a failed check must have an empty signature), SCRIPT_VERIFY_STRICTENC (strict encoding of keys and flags) and SCRIPT_VERIFY_DERSIG (strict DER, which is also in consensus), [True, True, True, True] (Bitcoin Core, 2026). This example reads core_src_policy_policy.h, a file saved with the chapter's evidence (the fetched sources, their test vectors or the record of Bitcoin Core 31.1.0's run), and a browser does not have it. Recorded output, produced when the chapter was built under Python 3.13.18 and not in your browser: [True, True, True, True]
nodes.definition: Bitcoin Core's standard policy flags include the low-S, null-fail, strict encoding and DER signature checks.

nodes.label: Cap on legacy signature operations
nodes.body: A signature operation is a use of a checking opcode such as OP_CHECKSIG, and in the legacy format each one makes the node hash a large part of the transaction. Bitcoin Core's policy header defines MAX_TX_LEGACY_SIGOPS as 2500 and BIP54, the consensus cleanup (status Complete), makes a transaction with strictly more than 2500 such operations invalid. The result is [2500, True]: the number in the source and the text in the BIP. Sergio Demian Lerner reported on 30 January 2013 'a transaction that takes at least 3 minutes to verify', recorded as CVE-2013-2292 (Bitcointalk, 2013). The release notes of Core 30.0 say the limit prepares for a possible BIP54 deployment, and the BIP states that the limit reduces the worst-case block validation time by a factor of 40 (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Poinsot and Corallo, 2025). This example reads core_src_policy_policy.h, a file saved with the chapter's evidence (the fetched sources, their test vectors or the record of Bitcoin Core 31.1.0's run), and a browser does not have it. Recorded output, produced when the chapter was built under Python 3.13.18 and not in your browser: [2500, True]
nodes.definition: Bitcoin Core 30.0 allows at most 2,500 potentially executed legacy signature operations in a standard transaction, the limit that BIP54 would make a consensus rule.

nodes.label: Inputs under the operation cap
nodes.body: The release notes of Bitcoin Core 30.0 say that the maximum number of potentially executed legacy signature operations in a single standard transaction is now limited to 2500, counting those in all previous output scripts, in all input scripts and in all P2SH redeem scripts (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The example turns the cap into a count of inputs: if each input executes 2 such operations, a quantity chosen only for the arithmetic, 2,500 divided by 2 gives 1,250 inputs with nothing left over, and a reader who sets 3 operations per input gets 833 with a remainder of 1. It is like a bridge with a weight limit: the limit is fixed, and how many vehicles pass depends on what each one weighs. The cap is a relay policy of the node, so a transaction above it is not relayed by default, which differs from a consensus rule that would make a block invalid.
nodes.example: a cap of 2,500 operations, 2 per input
nodes.definition: If every input of a standard transaction executes 2 legacy signature operations, the cap of 2,500 allows at most 1,250 such inputs.

nodes.label: Randomness and signature size
nodes.body: The nonce of a signature must be unpredictable to everyone and used once, because with a repeated or biased nonce the private key can be computed from the signatures; this branch shows the algebra of the recovery, the standard remedy of deriving the nonce deterministically from the key and the message (RFC 6979 for ECDSA and the default algorithm of BIP340 for schnorr), what Bitcoin Core does in practice (deterministic nonces, grinding for a small R, zero auxiliary data for taproot) and what that does to the size of signatures. Every behaviour is read from the software's source and confirmed by running it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Pornin, 2013).

nodes.label: Safety of the nonce
nodes.body: This group shows the consequence of repeating the nonce, the recovery of the private key from two signatures, and that the recovery needs the repetition (Breitner and Heninger, 2019).

nodes.label: Nonce reuse
nodes.body: The nonce k is a one-time secret, and the book's warning is that using it twice destroys the key. The reason is algebra. Two signatures on different hashes h1 and h2 with the same k have the same R, and s1 - s2 = k^-1 (h1 - h2), so k = (h1 - h2) / (s1 - s2); then from s1 = k^-1 (h1 + x R) the private key is x = (s1 k - h1) / R, all modulo n. The chapter signs two different payments with one nonce and recovers the key: the two R values are equal (True), the recovered key equals the private key (True) and the recovered nonce equals k (True), [True, True, True]. This is the failure mode in the Android story of 2013 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Breitner and Heninger, 2019).
nodes.definition: If two ECDSA signatures from the same key use the same nonce k, anyone can compute k and then the private key from the two signatures.

nodes.label: Distinct nonces
nodes.body: To show that the repetition is what the attack uses, the chapter applies the same recovery formula to two signatures that use different nonces and finds that the number it returns is not the private key, the answer False for 'equals the key'. A biased generator is also dangerous: Breitner and Heninger (2019) computed hundreds of Bitcoin private keys and dozens of Ethereum, Ripple, SSH and HTTPS private keys by attacking signatures in public blockchains and Internet-wide scans, and their method needs only that the nonce is not generated uniformly at random, which is why the standards ask for nonces that are random or derived from a hash of the secret and the message (Breitner and Heninger, 2019) (Pornin, 2013).
nodes.example: the same formula with two different nonces
nodes.definition: With two different nonces the same formula returns a number that is not the key, so the attack needs the repetition.

nodes.label: Recovering a key from a reused nonce
nodes.body: The book says that if the same value k is used with different messages, the signing private key can be calculated by anyone, and that people have had funds stolen because of an inadvertent reuse of k, most often through an improperly initialized random-number generator (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The algebra is short: subtracting the two signature equations leaves s1 - s2 = k^-1 (z1 - z2), so k = (z1 - z2) / (s1 - s2), and from the first equation x = (s1 k - z1) / r. In the example with the private key 17 and the nonce 29 modulo 101 the attacker, who sees only the two signatures and the two digests, recovers 29 and then 17. The reader can change the key, the nonce or the digests. It is like using the same one-time pad twice: the two messages together give away what each alone would hide. The value r is taken as given here, since only its reuse matters.
nodes.example: two signatures with one nonce reveal the key 17
nodes.definition: Two ECDSA signatures that use the same nonce k give k as the difference of the digests divided by the difference of the signature values, and then the private key.

nodes.label: Deterministic nonces
nodes.body: This group covers the cure, deriving the nonce from the key and the message: RFC 6979, the chapter's signer, and what Bitcoin Core does (Pornin, 2013).

nodes.label: RFC 6979 test vector
nodes.body: RFC 6979 (Pornin, 2013) specifies a way to derive the nonce k from the private key and the message hash with HMAC, a keyed hash, so that k is unpredictable to an attacker yet never repeats for different messages. The chapter implements the derivation and checks it against the vector in the RFC's appendix A.2.5 (the curve P-256, the message 'sample', SHA-256), read back from the saved text of the RFC: the derived k equals the published one, and its first hexadecimal digits are 0xa6e3c57d, [True, '0xa6e3c57d']. The same derivation works for secp256k1, which is where Bitcoin uses it (Pornin, 2013). This example reads rfc6979.txt, a file saved with the chapter's evidence (the fetched sources, their test vectors or the record of Bitcoin Core 31.1.0's run), and a browser does not have it. Recorded output, produced when the chapter was built under Python 3.13.18 and not in your browser: [True, '0xa6e3c57d']
nodes.definition: The chapter's implementation of the nonce derivation of RFC 6979 reproduces the nonce printed in the RFC's appendix for the curve P-256.
