nodes.label: Deterministic signing
nodes.body: A deterministic signer has the practical advantage that a test can compare signatures byte for byte, and the safety advantage that no random number is needed at signing time. The chapter signs the same message twice and gets identical signatures (True) and signs another message and gets a different one (True), [True, True]. The book recommends BIP340, RFC 6979 or a similar method and adds that extra entropy may be mixed in as protection against side-channel and fault attacks (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
nodes.definition: The chapter's ECDSA signer is deterministic: the same key and message give the same signature, another message gives another.

nodes.label: Library nonce matches the standard
nodes.body: To check that the signer does what it is said to do, the chapter derives the nonce with its own RFC 6979 function, signs with that nonce using the plain formulas of the book and compares the DER-encoded result with the signature produced by the library's signing function: they are equal (True), once the high s has been replaced by its negative. The library's signature therefore has no hidden randomness; it is a function of the key and the message (Pornin, 2013) (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
nodes.example: the same nonce as the standard gives
nodes.definition: The signature the chapter's signer makes is the one obtained from RFC 6979's nonce and the plain ECDSA formulas, normalized to low s.

nodes.label: Core signs deterministically
nodes.body: The regtest run signs the same unsigned transaction twice with the same wallet, once for a bech32 (ECDSA) input and once for a bech32m (schnorr) input, and compares the signed bytes. Both pairs are equal, [True, True]. In Bitcoin Core's source the ECDSA signing function calls the RFC 6979 nonce function, and the code that signs a taproot input contains the comment 'Use uint256{} as aux_rnd for now', so the auxiliary random data of BIP340 is the zero value; the book says only that BIP340 and RFC 6979 can be deterministic, so the actual setting of the reference software is a point it leaves out (Bitcoin Core, 2026). This example reads core_regtest_record_v1_0_0.json, a file saved with the chapter's evidence (the fetched sources, their test vectors or the record of Bitcoin Core 31.1.0's run), and a browser does not have it. Recorded output, produced when the chapter was built under Python 3.13.18 and not in your browser: [True, True]
nodes.definition: Bitcoin Core 31.1 gives the same signature when it signs the same transaction twice, for ECDSA and for taproot, because it derives the nonce deterministically and uses zero auxiliary data for schnorr.

nodes.label: Signature size and nonce grinding
nodes.body: This group covers the effect of the nonce on the length of ECDSA signatures and the grinding that Bitcoin Core does to keep them short (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

nodes.label: Low-R grinding
nodes.body: Because DER needs a padding byte whenever R's top bit is set, Bitcoin Core tries different nonces (its source says 'Grind for low R') until R is below 2 to the 255 and the signature is shorter by one byte. The chapter has the node sign a transaction with 300 inputs and finds the lengths of the 300 signatures with the hash type byte: 298 of 71 bytes and 2 of 70 bytes, summarized as [300, 71, 70, 300] (inputs, longest, shortest, count). All 300 verify with the chapter's code ([300, 300]) and all 300 have a low R ([300, 300]) (Bitcoin Core, 2026). This example reads core_regtest_record_v1_0_0.json, a file saved with the chapter's evidence (the fetched sources, their test vectors or the record of Bitcoin Core 31.1.0's run), and a browser does not have it. Recorded output, produced when the chapter was built under Python 3.13.18 and not in your browser: [300, 71, 70, 300]
nodes.definition: Bitcoin Core signs repeatedly until R is small, so all 300 signatures in a transaction with 300 inputs are 70 or 71 bytes with the hash type and none is longer.

nodes.label: High R without grinding
nodes.body: The grinding of Bitcoin Core is not a quirk: it is needed because a signer that does not grind produces 72-byte signatures half of the time. The chapter's own deterministic signer, which does not grind, made 400 signatures for 400 keys and messages, 197 of which had R at least 2 to the 255, which is between 40 and 60 percent of 400 (True): [400, 197, True]. Draft BIP 461 proposes to make the low-R grinding part of a standard deterministic ECDSA signature, so that signatures are at most 70 bytes when DER encoded (Gilligan, 2026).
nodes.example: about half have the top bit set
nodes.definition: A signer that does not grind produces a high R in about half of its signatures: of 400 signatures made by the chapter's library, 197 had the top bit of R set.

nodes.label: Grinding in the source
nodes.body: The behaviours reported in the previous leaves can be found in the source of the software at the commit the course pins. The saved key.cpp contains the comment 'Grind for low R' and the name secp256k1_nonce_function_rfc6979; the saved sign.cpp contains 'Use uint256{} as aux_rnd for now.' and the comment about the SIGHASH_SINGLE bug that ends 'So don't produce it.' The four tests return [True, True, True, True]. Reading the source does not replace the runs; the runs show that the released binary does what the source says (Bitcoin Core, 2026). This example reads core_src_key.cpp, a file saved with the chapter's evidence (the fetched sources, their test vectors or the record of Bitcoin Core 31.1.0's run), and a browser does not have it. Recorded output, produced when the chapter was built under Python 3.13.18 and not in your browser: [True, True, True, True]
nodes.definition: Bitcoin Core's key.cpp has the low-R grind and the RFC 6979 function, and sign.cpp has the zero auxiliary value and the refusal to produce the SINGLE bug signature.

nodes.label: Chance of a low R
nodes.body: Bitcoin Core signs, then checks the result with a function that returns true when the first byte of R is less than 0x80, and while it is not, it changes the extra entropy by a counter and signs again, which is the grinding for a low R (Bitcoin Core, 2026). A random first byte is below 0x80 in half the cases, so the chance that none of 8 attempts succeeds is one half to the power 8, which is 1 in 256, and the chance that at least one does is 0.9961; the reader can change the number of attempts and see how quickly certainty approaches. It is like tossing a coin until it shows heads: long runs of tails are rare, so the loop ends after about two tries on average. A low R avoids the padding zero of the previous DER example, which is why Bitcoin Core's signatures are 70 or 71 bytes and the book's sample is 72.
nodes.example: the chance to find a low R within 8 attempts
nodes.definition: Because a low R is a first byte below 0x80, each attempt succeeds with a chance of one half, so 8 attempts succeed with a chance of 0.9961 and at most 256 values of the counter need to be considered.

nodes.label: Segwit signing
nodes.body: Segregated witness changed how the data that is signed is built, and this branch collects the two consequences that the chapter's last section and the later BIPs describe: the cost of verifying a transaction with many inputs, which grew with the square of the number of inputs in the old algorithm and grows linearly in the BIP143 algorithm, and the commitment of the signature to the amount of the coin being spent (and, in BIP341, to all the amounts), which the old algorithm did not give. It ends with taproot signing, where the chapter checks a real key-path spend and the verdicts of Bitcoin Core on malformed schnorr signatures (Lau and Wuille, 2016) (Wuille et al., 2020).

nodes.label: Cost of hashing
nodes.body: This group counts the bytes hashed by the legacy and BIP143 algorithms to show the quadratic and the linear growth (Lau and Wuille, 2016).

nodes.label: Quadratic hashing
nodes.body: Each of the n inputs of a legacy transaction needs a signature check, and each check hashes a copy of the transaction that is about n inputs long, so the total work is about n squared. The chapter counts the bytes passed to SHA-256 for transactions with 1, 10, 100 and 1,000 inputs and one output: for the legacy algorithm 146, 5,150, 420,500 and 41,107,000 bytes, and for the BIP143 algorithm 384, 2,670, 25,530 and 254,130. BIP143 hashes the shared parts once and reuses them, so the work is proportional to n: the second column is [[1, 146, 384], [10, 5150, 2670], [100, 420500, 25530], [1000, 41107000, 254130]]. For a single input the new algorithm hashes more bytes, but for large transactions it is far cheaper (Lau and Wuille, 2016) (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
nodes.definition: In the legacy algorithm every signature check hashes nearly the whole transaction, so the bytes hashed grow with the square of the number of inputs; BIP143 hashes each part once.

nodes.label: Growth of hashing
nodes.body: The book says the hash operations of the legacy algorithm increase 'roughly quadratically' and those of BIP143 'in O(n)'. The two growth factors from 100 to 1,000 inputs are [97.8, 10.0]: ten times the inputs cost about ninety-eight times the hashing in the legacy algorithm, which is almost the hundredfold of a perfect square law, and exactly ten times in the BIP143 algorithm. BIP143 itself says a 1 MB transaction with 5,569 signature operations may take 25 seconds to verify under the old algorithm (Lau and Wuille, 2016).
nodes.definition: Going from 100 to 1,000 inputs multiplies the legacy work by 97.8 and the segwit work by 10.0.

nodes.label: Bytes hashed grow with inputs
nodes.body: The book warns that in the old algorithm the hash operations increase roughly quadratically with the number of inputs, so that an attacker can build a transaction that costs a node a great deal of hashing (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023), and BIP143 states that the amount of hashing for each signature is proportional to the size of the transaction, so that hashing grows in O(n squared) with the number of signature operations, and that a reusable intermediate hash brings it to O(n) (Lau and Wuille, 2016). The example models a transaction of k inputs of an assumed 148 bytes each plus 100 fixed bytes, hashed once for every input: 10 inputs hash 15,800 bytes, 20 inputs hash 61,200 bytes, and the ratio 3.87 is close to the factor 4 that squaring predicts. It is like a teacher who rereads the whole class register for every student who signs it: doubling the class does not double the work but nearly quadruples it. The sizes are assumptions chosen for the arithmetic, not measurements.
nodes.example: doubling the inputs roughly quadruples the bytes hashed
nodes.definition: If each of n signatures hashes about the whole transaction, and the transaction grows with n, the bytes hashed grow with n squared: 20 inputs cost about 3.9 times what 10 inputs cost.

io.code: n = 10; per = 148; fixed = 100; h = lambda k: k * (k * per + fixed); (h(n), h(2 * n), round(h(2 * n) / h(n), 2))

nodes.label: Twenty-five seconds for 5,569 operations
nodes.body: BIP143 gives the measured motivation for the new algorithm: in 2015 a 1 MB block would normally take 2 seconds to verify with an average computer, while a 1 MB transaction with 5,569 signature operations may take 25 seconds (Lau and Wuille, 2016). The example divides the two times, which shows the single transaction to be 12.5 times slower than a whole ordinary block, and divides the 25 seconds by the number of operations, which gives 4.5 milliseconds for each signature check when every check rehashes a megabyte; the reader can change the seconds or the number of operations. It is like a postal clerk who must photocopy the entire parcel before stamping each of thousands of labels. The figures belong to the computer and the year named by the BIP and say nothing about today's hardware, but the ratio explains why Bitcoin Core later capped legacy signature operations.
nodes.definition: BIP143 reports that a block of 1 MB takes about 2 seconds to verify but a 1 MB transaction with 5,569 signature operations may take 25 seconds, about 4.5 milliseconds for each operation.

io.code: sigops = 5569; secs = 25; block = 2; (round(secs / block, 1), round(secs * 1000 / sigops, 1))

nodes.label: Commitment to amounts
nodes.body: This group shows the commitment of signatures to the value of the coins, which BIP143 introduced and BIP341 extended (Wuille et al., 2020).

nodes.label: Commitment to the amount (BIP143)
nodes.body: In the legacy algorithm the signer sees the previous output's script but not its value, so a signer who does not have the previous transaction cannot know from the signature hash how much the coin is worth and therefore how large the fee is. BIP143 states that every signature hash type commits to the amount being spent, and puts the amount of the input into the hash, and the chapter shows that changing the amount by one satoshi changes the digest (True). The book's segwit section does not mention this, and a note in its source says that the coverage of values to help hardware wallets still has to be written (Lau and Wuille, 2016) (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
nodes.example: a segwit signature covers the amount
nodes.definition: In BIP143 the signature hash includes the amount of the coin being spent, so a signer cannot be tricked about the amount, which the legacy hash does not offer.

nodes.label: Commitment to all amounts (BIP341)
nodes.body: BIP341 extends the idea: the signature message includes the amounts and the scripts of all the outputs being spent, which is the kind of coverage the editor's note in the book's source hopes will help hardware wallets. The chapter changes the amount of the second input and finds that the digest of the first input changes under the default hash type (True), and does not change under ANYONECANPAY (True): [True, True]. The consequence is that taproot spenders who use the common default or SIGHASH_ALL commit to the whole picture of the transaction (Wuille et al., 2020).
nodes.definition: A taproot signature commits to the amounts of all inputs being spent, unless ANYONECANPAY is used, when it commits only to its own.

nodes.label: Taproot signing
nodes.body: This group checks a real taproot signature from the main chain and the verdicts of Bitcoin Core on altered ones (Wuille et al., 2020).

nodes.label: A first taproot spend
nodes.body: The taproot soft fork took effect at block 709,632 on 14 November 2021, and the transaction 33e794d0... is recorded as the first spend of a taproot output through the key path; this package did not check that no earlier one exists. The chapter checks the saved record of that transaction and finds the block height 709,635, one item in the witness, a signature of 64 bytes (the default hash type), and that the schnorr signature verifies against the key of the spent output with the BIP341 signature message: [709635, 1, 64, True]. The record gives its time as 2021-11-14 05:40:13 UTC (Mempool Space, 2026) (Wuille et al., 2020). This example reads mainnet_tx_33e794d0.json, a file saved with the chapter's evidence (the fetched sources, their test vectors or the record of Bitcoin Core 31.1.0's run), and a browser does not have it. Recorded output, produced when the chapter was built under Python 3.13.18 and not in your browser: [709635, 1, 64, True]
nodes.definition: The taproot key-path spend recorded as the first on the main chain has a one-element witness holding a 64-byte schnorr signature, which verifies with the chapter's code.

nodes.label: Core's taproot verdicts
nodes.body: On the private test network, the chapter signs a taproot input with its own key and tests six variants of the signature with testmempoolaccept: the 64-byte default is allowed, and so is the 65-byte signature with the explicit hash type 0x01; the 65-byte signature with the explicit value 0x00 is refused with 'Invalid Schnorr signature hash type'; the 63-byte one with 'Invalid Schnorr signature size'; a signature with one flipped bit and a signature whose hash type does not match the one it was made with are refused with 'Invalid Schnorr signature'. The book says an explicit SIGHASH_ALL wastes a byte; it does not say that an explicit 0x00 is not allowed (Wuille et al., 2020) (Bitcoin Core, 2026). This example reads core_regtest_record_v1_0_0.json, a file saved with the chapter's evidence (the fetched sources, their test vectors or the record of Bitcoin Core 31.1.0's run), and a browser does not have it. Recorded output, produced when the chapter was built under Python 3.13.18 and not in your browser: {'default_64': [True, None], 'explicit_all_65': [True, None], 'explicit_zero_65': [False, 'mempool-script-verify-flag-failed (Invalid Schnorr signature hash type)'], 'short_63': [False, 'mempool-script-verify-flag-failed (Invalid Schnorr signature size)'], 'flipped_bit': [False, 'mempool-script-verify-flag-failed (Invalid Schnorr signature)'], 'hash_type_mismatch': [False, 'mempool-script-verify-flag-failed (Invalid Schnorr signature)']}
nodes.example: what the node says about five malformed signatures
nodes.definition: Bitcoin Core 31.1 accepts the 64-byte default and the explicit ALL signature and rejects an explicit zero hash type, a 63-byte signature and two altered signatures, each with its own message.

nodes.label: Activation on a retarget boundary
nodes.body: BIP341 states that the minimum activation height of taproot is block 709632 and that the deployment did activate at that height on Bitcoin mainnet (Wuille et al., 2020), and the record of the first taproot key-path spend in the saved mainnet data puts it in block 709,635 (Mempool Space, 2026). The example divides the activation height by the 2,016 blocks of a difficulty period, giving 352 with remainder 0, so the activation fell on a period boundary, and subtracts to find that the first spend came 3 blocks later. The reader can change the heights. It is like a school year that always begins on the first day of a term: upgrades that count in periods start where the counting turns over. The same record is checked by the chapter's earlier example that verifies this spend's signature.
nodes.example: taproot's activation height is a multiple of 2016
nodes.definition: Block 709,632 is exactly 352 retarget periods of 2,016 blocks after the genesis block, and the first taproot spend followed it by 3 blocks.

io.code: act = 709632; first = 709635; p = 2016; (act // p, act % p, first - act)

nodes.label: Since the book went to print
nodes.body: The 3rd edition went to print in 2023 and some of its statements have moved: proposals have changed status, Bitcoin Core has added support for MuSig2 and a limit on signature operations, a threshold signature BIP has been proposed, the library has changed an interface, and two new drafts concern ECDSA and the quantum threat. This branch collects those changes with their sources, adds the dates of the history the chapter touches (the patent, the book's real transaction, the taproot activation) and records how the evidence of the package was gathered, so that each statement can be traced to a saved copy of its source (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Bitcoin Optech, 2026).

nodes.label: Status of the standards
nodes.body: This group states the present status of the proposals and the support in Bitcoin Core that the book describes as future or does not mention (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

nodes.label: Status of the BIPs
nodes.body: A BIP, a Bitcoin Improvement Proposal, has a status that says how far it has gone. Reading the index of the BIPs repository at the pinned commit, the chapter finds: 66 (strict DER), 143 (segwit signing), 327 (MuSig2), 340, 341 and 342 (schnorr, taproot and tapscript) Deployed; 146 (signature malleability) Closed; 373 (MuSig2 fields of PSBT) and 54 (consensus cleanup) Complete; and 118 (ANYPREVOUT), 390 (the musig descriptor), 461 (deterministic ECDSA) and 361 (post-quantum sunset) Draft. A Draft is a proposal that anyone may change or that may never be deployed, so it must not be described as part of Bitcoin (Bitcoin BIPs, 2026) (Wuille et al., 2020). This example reads bips_README.mediawiki, a file saved with the chapter's evidence (the fetched sources, their test vectors or the record of Bitcoin Core 31.1.0's run), and a browser does not have it. Recorded output, produced when the chapter was built under Python 3.13.18 and not in your browser: {66: 'Deployed', 118: 'Draft', 143: 'Deployed', 146: 'Closed', 327: 'Deployed', 340: 'Deployed', 341: 'Deployed', 342: 'Deployed', 373: 'Complete', 390: 'Draft', 54: 'Complete', 461: 'Draft', 361: 'Draft'}
nodes.definition: In the BIP index, 66, 143, 327, 340, 341 and 342 are Deployed, 146 is Closed, 373 and 54 are Complete, and 118, 390, 461 and 361 are Drafts.

nodes.label: musig() in Bitcoin Core
nodes.body: A descriptor is Bitcoin Core's text format for describing which keys and scripts make up addresses. The saved documentation of Core's list of implemented BIPs says that BIP327 key aggregation through the musig() descriptor is supported as of v30.0 and signing as of v31.0, and the saved descriptor documentation shows that the version 29.0 file has tr(KEY) but no mention of musig, while the version 31.0 file does. The five checks return [True, True, True, True, True]. For a student this means that the scriptless multisignature of the book can now be created with a standard wallet command (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Chow, 2024). This example reads core_doc_bips.md, a file saved with the chapter's evidence (the fetched sources, their test vectors or the record of Bitcoin Core 31.1.0's run), and a browser does not have it. Recorded output, produced when the chapter was built under Python 3.13.18 and not in your browser: [True, True, True, True, True]
nodes.definition: Bitcoin Core 30.0 added the musig() descriptor and the MuSig2 fields of PSBT, 31.0 added signing, and the descriptor documentation of 29.0 does not have it.

nodes.label: BIPs listed by Bitcoin Core
nodes.body: The list in Bitcoin Core's doc/bips.md is the project's own answer to which proposals it implements. Reading the saved copy at the pinned commit, the BIPs 66, 143, 327, 340, 373 and 390 appear, and 118, 54, 461 and 361 do not: {66: True, 143: True, 327: True, 340: True, 373: True, 390: True, 118: False, 54: False, 461: False, 361: False}. The absence of BIP 54 fits its status: Core 30.0 prepared the ground with the 2,500-operation relay limit, but the consensus change is not deployed (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Poinsot and Corallo, 2025). This example reads core_doc_bips.md, a file saved with the chapter's evidence (the fetched sources, their test vectors or the record of Bitcoin Core 31.1.0's run), and a browser does not have it. Recorded output, produced when the chapter was built under Python 3.13.18 and not in your browser: {66: True, 143: True, 327: True, 340: True, 373: True, 390: True, 118: False, 54: False, 461: False, 361: False}
nodes.definition: Bitcoin Core's list of implemented BIPs has 66, 143, 327, 340, 373 and 390 and does not have the drafts 118, 461 and 361 or BIP 54.

nodes.label: No threshold BIP
nodes.body: The book states that no scriptless threshold signature protocol had been proposed as a BIP. The chapter looks in the saved index of the BIPs repository for the word FROST (not found, False) and for the word threshold (found once, in the title of an unrelated soft-fork activation proposal, 'Reduced threshold Segwit MASF', True), and in the saved Optech topic page finds the 2024 mention 'BIP proposed for creating FROST scriptless threshold signatures for Bitcoin' (True): [False, 1, True, True]. So the sentence of the book is a snapshot of 2023 and a proposal exists but has no number in the index. FROST itself is a published threshold scheme (Komlo and Goldberg, 2021) (Bitcoin Optech, 2026). This example reads bips_README.mediawiki, a file saved with the chapter's evidence (the fetched sources, their test vectors or the record of Bitcoin Core 31.1.0's run), and a browser does not have it. Recorded output, produced when the chapter was built under Python 3.13.18 and not in your browser: [False, 1, True, True]
nodes.example: no threshold BIP in the index
nodes.definition: The BIP index has no entry for a threshold signature scheme, while Optech lists a 2024 mention of a BIP proposed for FROST.

nodes.label: Library and release support
nodes.body: This group records changes in the library and the release that implements the signatures, which are the places where the book's text has aged (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

nodes.label: Changes in libsecp256k1
nodes.body: libsecp256k1 is the C library that Bitcoin Core uses for every signature and key operation described in this chapter. Its changelog, saved from the pinned commit, has a version 0.8.0 dated 2026-08-03 (True) that lists 'Removed previously deprecated function alias secp256k1_schnorrsig_sign' (True), and Bitcoin Core's key.cpp calls secp256k1_schnorrsig_sign32 (True): [True, True, True]. The alias was kept for older programs; its removal does not change the signatures but is a reminder that a library's interface is a moving target (Bitcoin Core, 2026). This example reads secp256k1_CHANGELOG.md, a file saved with the chapter's evidence (the fetched sources, their test vectors or the record of Bitcoin Core 31.1.0's run), and a browser does not have it. Recorded output, produced when the chapter was built under Python 3.13.18 and not in your browser: [True, True, True]
nodes.definition: The secp256k1 library removed its deprecated function alias for schnorr signing in version 0.8.0, and Bitcoin Core calls the function with the name secp256k1_schnorrsig_sign32.

nodes.label: Release note of Core 30.0
nodes.body: The statement is read from the saved release notes of Core 30.0: 'The maximum number of potentially executed legacy signature operations in a single standard transaction is now limited to 2500' and 'The change was done to prepare for a possible BIP54 deployment in the future'. Both sentences are present (True). The limit is policy and not consensus, so a miner can still include a transaction above it, and the cap tells wallet authors what transactions will propagate (Bitcoin Core, 2026). This example reads core_release_30.0_notes.txt, a file saved with the chapter's evidence (the fetched sources, their test vectors or the record of Bitcoin Core 31.1.0's run), and a browser does not have it. Recorded output, produced when the chapter was built under Python 3.13.18 and not in your browser: True
nodes.example: a limit in the release notes
nodes.definition: The release notes of Bitcoin Core 30.0 state the limit of 2,500 legacy signature operations and name BIP54 as the reason.

nodes.label: History and dates
nodes.body: This group gives the dates behind the chapter's history, the patent, the book's real transaction and the taproot activation, each computed or read from a saved source (Cornell Legal Information Institute, 2026).

nodes.label: Patent dates
nodes.body: For United States applications filed before the cut-off of 1995 that the statute names, a patent lasted the greater of 17 years from grant and 20 years from filing. For the Schnorr patent the dates in the patent record are the filing date 1990-02-23 and the publication date 1991-02-19. The chapter computes 17 years from the grant as 2008-02-19 and 20 years from the filing as 2010-02-23, and finds that the second is later (True); Wikipedia states that the patent expired in February 2010 (Wikipedia, 2026), and the patent record shows the status 'Expired - Lifetime' (True), though the site marks it as an assumption, not a legal conclusion, and the Cornell text of the statute has the rule (True): ['2008-02-19', '2010-02-23', True, True, True]. This is consistent with the book's 'almost two decades' (USPTO, 1991) (Cornell Legal Information Institute, 2026). This example reads google_patent_US4995082.txt, a file saved with the chapter's evidence (the fetched sources, their test vectors or the record of Bitcoin Core 31.1.0's run), and a browser does not have it. Recorded output, produced when the chapter was built under Python 3.13.18 and not in your browser: ['2008-02-19', '2010-02-23', True, True, True]
nodes.example: 17 years from grant or 20 from filing
nodes.definition: Schnorr's patent 4,995,082 was filed on 23 February 1990 and published on 19 February 1991, so the statute's greater term ends on 23 February 2010.

nodes.label: Years from Schnorr to taproot
nodes.body: The scheme was described by Claus-Peter Schnorr at Crypto '89, published in the proceedings in 1990 and in the Journal of Cryptology in January 1991, and it became part of Bitcoin's rules at block 709,632 on 14 November 2021. The subtraction of years gives [30, 32] (from 1991 and from 1989). Pieter Wuille posted the first public draft of a BIP for 64-byte schnorr signatures to the bitcoin-dev mailing list on 6 July 2018 (Wuille, 2018), and BIP340 was assigned its number on 2020-01-19 (Wuille et al., 2020). Bitcoin began in January 2009, so the activation came 4,698 days after the genesis block, and the choice of ECDSA in 2009 was made at a time when the patent was still in force (Schnorr, 1991) (Schnorr, 1990).
nodes.definition: Thirty years separate the publication of Schnorr's journal paper in 1991 from the activation of schnorr signatures in Bitcoin in 2021, and 32 years the Crypto '89 priority.

nodes.label: Time of the book's transaction
nodes.body: The block time recorded by the explorer for block 277,316 is the Unix time 1388185914, which the chapter converts to the date '2013-12-27 23:11:54' in UTC. A block time is set by the miner, within the limits of the rules, and is not an exact clock, so the sentence is accurate to within minutes or hours rather than seconds (Mempool Space, 2026). This example reads mainnet_tx_0627052b.json, a file saved with the chapter's evidence (the fetched sources, their test vectors or the record of Bitcoin Core 31.1.0's run), and a browser does not have it. Recorded output, produced when the chapter was built under Python 3.13.18 and not in your browser: '2013-12-27 23:11:54'
nodes.definition: The transaction whose signature the book prints was mined on 27 December 2013 at 23:11:54 UTC.

nodes.label: Days to taproot
nodes.body: Counting days from the genesis block on 3 January 2009 to 14 November 2021, the day of the taproot activation at block 709,632, gives 4,698 days, about 12 years and 10 months. It is the length of time during which ECDSA was the only signature algorithm of Bitcoin, which the book states as 'until the activation of the taproot soft fork in 2021' (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
nodes.definition: Taproot took effect 4,698 days after the genesis block of 3 January 2009.

nodes.label: The patent term in years
nodes.body: Schnorr's United States patent 4,995,082 was filed on 23 February 1990 and granted on 19 February 1991 (USPTO, 1991), and the statute gives a term that ends 20 years from the date on which the application was filed (Cornell Legal Information Institute, 2026), and for patents of that age the term is the greater of the 20-year term and 17 years from grant (Cornell Legal Information Institute, 2026), which would end in 2008, so the later date, 2010, governs. Wikipedia agrees that the patent expired in February 2010 (Wikipedia, 2026). The example computes both and takes the larger, and the reader can change the years or the terms. It is like a ticket that is valid for the later of two printed expiry dates. This arithmetic explains why the book can say that the patent kept the algorithm out of open standards for almost two decades, and why a signature scheme from 1989 could enter Bitcoin only in 2021.
nodes.example: filed 1990, granted 1991: the term ends in 2010
nodes.definition: A patent filed in 1990 and granted in 1991 ran to the greater of 20 years from filing, 2010, and 17 years from grant, 2008, which is 2010.

nodes.body: This group describes how the package's evidence was gathered and kept: the sources, the node run and the release checksum (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The record says [66, 66, 214, 214]: 66 sources, 66 answered with status 200, 214 passages to find and 214 found. nodes.body: Regtest is Bitcoin Core's regression test mode, a private chain on one computer where blocks can be created at will; nothing in it touches the Bitcoin network. The record of the run states the node version 310100, the subversion '/Satoshi:31.1.0/' and the chain 'regtest': [310100, '/Satoshi:31.1.0/', 'regtest']. The numbers come from one run on 15 October 2026 and are stored as a JSON file that the chapter's verification program reads offline, so a reader can repeat the checks without a node (Bitcoin Core, 2026). nodes.label: Checksum of the release

findings: Background

Chapter 8 of the 3rd edition explains what a digital signature is for in Bitcoin, how a signature commits to a chosen part of a transaction through the SIGHASH flag, how the schnorr algorithm works and what it makes possible (multisignatures and threshold signatures that look like one signature), how ECDSA, the signature Bitcoin used until 2021, works and is serialized, why the random nonce must never repeat, and how segwit changed what is hashed; this package recomputes its figures and examples and checks the statements that moved since print (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
Comparative analysis

The book says that the arithmetic of the schnorr and ECDSA equations is performed modulo p, the prime of the field; the scalars of the signature equations (the nonce, the challenge, the private key and the value s) are instead reduced modulo n, the order of the group of points, which is a different number: the equation sG = kG + eX holds when s is reduced modulo n and fails when it is reduced modulo p, and BIP340 and SEC 2 give both numbers separately (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Wuille et al., 2020) (SECG, 2010).
Comparative analysis

The book's table of SIGHASH flags says SINGLE signs 'the one output with the same index number as the signed input', but not what happens when there is no such output: in the legacy signature hash the function returns the number one instead of a hash, which is the SIGHASH_SINGLE bug that Bitcoin Core's source marks and that the Bitcoin Wiki describes, and Bitcoin Core 31.1 refuses to sign such an input, leaving it unsigned with an error, while it signs the same transaction when each input has an output (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Bitcoin Wiki, 2026).
Comparative analysis

The book's table says ALL, NONE and SINGLE sign 'all inputs', which is true of the outpoints (which coins are spent) but not of the other inputs' sequence numbers: the executed probe shows that, as BIP143 specifies for segwit version 0 and the legacy algorithm does too, the sequence numbers of other inputs are left out of the hash under NONE and SINGLE as well as under ANYONECANPAY (Lau and Wuille, 2016).
Comparative analysis

The book's segwit section describes only the quadratic hashing and its O(n) repair; it does not say what else BIP143 changed, and it carries an unfinished editor's note about values: BIP143 makes every segwit version 0 signature commit to the amount of the coin being spent, which the legacy hash never does, and BIP341 goes further and commits to the amounts and scripts of all inputs unless ANYONECANPAY is used, which is what lets a hardware wallet check the fee without seeing the previous transactions (Lau and Wuille, 2016) (Wuille et al., 2020).
Comparative analysis

The 72-byte signature printed in the book's DER section is a real mainnet signature from block 277,316 (27 December 2013); it verifies against the transaction's legacy signature hash, and it is long because its R value begins with the byte 0x88 and so needs a padding zero, whereas Bitcoin Core grinds the nonce until R is small, and the 300 signatures that Core 31.1 made in one transaction are all 70 or 71 bytes (298 of 71 and 2 of 70, with the hash type byte) and all low-R (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).
Comparative analysis

The book does not separate the signature rules that are consensus from those that are only policy: Bitcoin Core accepts a transaction with a high-S signature in a block (the rule of BIP146 is policy, so nodes do not relay it) while a signature that is not strictly DER encoded makes the block invalid (a consensus rule since BIP66 and the July 2015 soft fork), as the regtest run shows by mining both (Lau and Wuille, 2016) (Wuille, 2015).
Comparative analysis

The book says the 65-byte taproot signature carries an explicit hash type; BIP341 makes the explicit value 0x00 invalid (the default is the absence of the byte), so the only valid explicit values are 0x01, 0x02, 0x03, 0x81, 0x82 and 0x83, and Bitcoin Core 31.1 rejects a 65-byte signature ending in 00 with 'Invalid Schnorr signature hash type' and a 63-byte signature with 'Invalid Schnorr signature size' while accepting the 64-byte default and the explicit ALL (Wuille et al., 2020).
Comparative analysis

The book's statement that Schnorr's patent kept the algorithm out of open standards for almost two decades fits the dates: United States patent 4,995,082 was filed on 23 February 1990 and published on 19 February 1991, the statute gave a patent of that age the greater of 20 years from filing (23 February 2010) and 17 years from grant (19 February 2008), and Wikipedia says it expired in February 2010; the paper itself appeared in the proceedings of Crypto '89 (1990) and in the Journal of Cryptology in 1991 (USPTO, 1991) (Cornell Legal Information Institute, 2026).
Comparative analysis

The book's identification protocol and the signature built from it by the Fiat-Shamir transform reproduce on secp256k1: with a fresh challenge the verifier's equation holds, with a changed response it fails, an impersonator who is told the challenge before committing can pass without the private key, and the signature with the challenge replaced by a hash of the commitment, key and message verifies for its message and fails for another, which is the construction of Fiat and Shamir (1986) and Schnorr (1991) (Fiat and Shamir, 1986) (Schnorr, 1991).
Comparative analysis

The book's claim that schnorr signatures can be batch verified in about half the time of single verification rests on the linearity of the signature equation, which reproduces (the combined equation accepts the nine valid signatures of the BIP340 vectors and rejects the batch with one signature swapped), but the speed-up is not reproduced here because the libsecp256k1 README lists no batch verification API; BIP342 introduces OP_CHECKSIGADD precisely so that multisignature policies in tapscript stay batch verifiable (Wuille et al., 2020) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).
Comparative analysis

The numbers of the chapter's equations can be recomputed from whole numbers that a reader may change, and eighteen worked examples do so: the ECDSA equations and the identity proof hold line for line in the integers modulo 101 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023); a first byte of 136 gives the padding zero that makes the book's signature 71 bytes before the hash type (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023); a flag byte of 131 is SINGLE with ANYONECANPAY (Bitcoin Core, 2026); 5,569 signature operations took 25 seconds, 4.5 milliseconds each (Lau and Wuille, 2016); the cap of 2,500 allows 1,250 inputs of 2 operations each (Bitcoin Core, 2026); a low R is found within 8 attempts with a chance of 0.9961 (Bitcoin Core, 2026); schnorr saves 9 bytes of witness for each input (Wuille et al., 2020); two signatures with one nonce give away the key (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023); and the patent of 1990 ran to 2010 (Cornell Legal Information Institute, 2026).
Conclusion

For the course, a signature is the unit of authorization of a transaction, and the chapter's evidence shows how far it can be reproduced: every flag, every signature length, every encoding rule and the key recovery attack recompute from the standards and Bitcoin Core 31.1 on regtest, while the full security proof of ECDSA, the speed of batch verification, quantum attacks and the behaviour of other Core releases are not reproduced here (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
Conclusion

The worked examples of version 1.2.0 carry their limits with them: the toy examples use the integers modulo 101 in place of curve points, so they show the algebra and not the secrecy, because division is possible there and impossible on secp256k1 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023); the sizes of the hashing model, 148 bytes for each input and 100 fixed bytes, and the 2 operations for each input under the cap are assumptions chosen for the arithmetic and not measurements; the 25 seconds were measured by the authors of BIP143 on the computer of 2015 and say nothing about today (Lau and Wuille, 2016); and the first taproot spend is the one in the saved mainnet record (Mempool Space, 2026).
Contemporary developments

Bitcoin Core derives the ECDSA nonce with the deterministic function of RFC 6979 and grinds it for a small R, and it signs a taproot input with an all-zero auxiliary random value for now, so that signing the same transaction twice gives the same signature in both cases, which the regtest run confirms; the book says only that BIP340 and RFC 6979 can be deterministic (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Pornin, 2013).
Contemporary developments

The book calls scriptless multisignatures an application of linearity that needs protection against key cancellation; the protection now exists as a standard: BIP327 (MuSig2) is Deployed, its key aggregation reproduces its four test vectors here, and a rogue key of the form 'my key minus yours' no longer gives the attacker control of the aggregate, while Bitcoin Core supports the musig() descriptor from version 30.0 and signing with it from version 31.0 (Nick et al., 2022) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).
Contemporary developments

The book says no scriptless threshold signature protocol has been proposed as a BIP; the BIP index at the pinned commit still has no number for one, but Bitcoin Optech's topic page lists 'BIP proposed for creating FROST scriptless threshold signatures for Bitcoin' among its 2024 mentions and the FROST scheme itself was published in 2021, so the book's statement is a snapshot of 2023, and MuSig2 remains an n-of-n scheme and not a threshold scheme (Bitcoin Optech, 2026) (Komlo and Goldberg, 2021).
Contemporary developments

The book names BIP118, SIGHASH_ANYPREVOUT, as a proposal; it is still a Draft in the BIP index and Bitcoin Core does not list it among the BIPs it implements, and Bitcoin Optech describes it as an updated version of SIGHASH_NOINPUT used by eltoo (Decker and Towns, 2017) (Bitcoin Optech, 2026).
Contemporary developments

Bitcoin Core 30.0 made standard transactions with more than 2,500 potentially executed legacy signature operations non-standard, to prepare for BIP54, the consensus cleanup (Complete), which would make such a transaction invalid; the cap answers the long verification times of crafted legacy transactions of the kind CVE-2013-2292 named, and BIP54 states that its limit reduces the worst-case block validation time by a factor of 40, while CVE-2013-2292 is the earlier example of a transaction that takes minutes to verify (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Poinsot and Corallo, 2025) (Bitcoin Wiki, 2026).
Contemporary developments

A Draft BIP 461 (2026) proposes deterministic ECDSA signatures with low-R grinding, so that signatures are at most 70 bytes when DER encoded instead of 72, and a Draft BIP 361 (2026) proposes a pre-announced sunset of legacy ECDSA and schnorr signatures as a migration to post-quantum signatures; both are proposals, neither is deployed, and the book has nothing on either (Gilligan, 2026) (Lopp et al., 2026).
Contemporary developments

The 2013 weakness of the random number generator of Android, announced to Bitcoin users on 11 August 2013 and explained by the Android security team on 14 August, is the real-world case for the chapter's randomness section; the sources name the improper initialization of the generator but not the exact flaw that was exploited, while the chapter shows that two ECDSA signatures with one nonce give away the private key and that the deterministic nonce of RFC 6979 removes the need for a good generator at signing time (Bitcoin.org, 2013) (Klyubin, 2013).
Contemporary developments

The libsecp256k1 library that Bitcoin Core uses for all of this removed the previously deprecated function alias secp256k1_schnorrsig_sign in version 0.8.0 (3 August 2026), and Bitcoin Core's key code calls secp256k1_schnorrsig_sign32; the book's description of schnorr signing is independent of that change but a reader of the library's header will meet the new name (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

stories.title: The signature that was patented for two decades
stories.who: Claus-Peter Schnorr, the cryptographer who invented the signature; the company Public Key Partners, which the patent database lists as its later holder
stories.where: the United States patent office for United States patent 4,995,082, applied for on 23 February 1990 with a priority date of 24 February 1989, and the Crypto '89 conference whose proceedings published his scheme
stories.story: Claus-Peter Schnorr published an efficient identification and signature scheme for smart cards in the proceedings of the Crypto '89 conference, and the United States published his patent 4,995,082 on 19 February 1991, filed on 23 February 1990 and claiming priority from 24 February 1989. Public Key Partners, which the patent database lists as its later holder, kept the algorithm out of open standards, so cryptographers of the early 1990s who wanted a free alternative designed the Digital Signature Algorithm and its elliptic curve version, ECDSA, and ECDSA was the only signature Bitcoin supported from its first release until the taproot soft fork of 2021. The statute gave such a patent the greater of 17 years from grant, 19 February 2008, and 20 years from filing, 23 February 2010; the chapter computes both, and Wikipedia states that the patent expired in February 2010, which fits the book's 'almost two decades'. The BIP340 signature that Bitcoin uses today is Schnorr's scheme in a form made for its curve, and the chapter checks it against the 19 official test vectors.
stories.lesson: A patent decided which signature Bitcoin started with

stories.title: When the phone's random numbers were not random
stories.who: Alex Klyubin, the Android security engineer who explained the cause; the Bitcoin Wallet, blockchain.info, BitcoinSpinner and Mycelium Wallet teams that released updates; Soo Hyeon Kim, Daewan Han and Dong Hoon Lee, who reported the flaw to Google
stories.where: Android phones worldwide, and the Bitcoin.org network alert; Android Developers Blog, 14 August 2013
stories.story: On 11 August 2013 Bitcoin.org published an alert that the Android component that generates secure random numbers contained critical weaknesses, which made every wallet generated on Android vulnerable to theft, and named Bitcoin Wallet, blockchain.info, BitcoinSpinner and Mycelium Wallet; Bitcoin Wallet 3.15 rotated keys automatically. Soo Hyeon Kim, Daewan Han and Dong Hoon Lee had reported the flaw to Google, and on 14 August the Android security engineer Alex Klyubin wrote that the cause was an improper initialization of the underlying pseudo-random number generator, that the investigation had begun with the compromise of one bitcoin transaction, and that developers should seed it from /dev/urandom. The sources do not say which flaw the thief used; the chapter shows why such a weakness is fatal for signatures: when two ECDSA signatures from one key share a nonce, the private key follows from a few modular subtractions and divisions, and the chapter's script recovers a test key that way. This is why the book asks for the deterministic nonce of RFC 6979 and why Bitcoin Core now derives its nonces from the key and the message.

stories.story: The long hexadecimal string that Andreas M. Antonopoulos and David A. Harding printed in chapter 8 of Mastering Bitcoin to explain the DER layout, beginning 3045022100884d142d, is not an invented example: it is the signature in the input of transaction 0627052b6f28912f2703066a912ea577f2ce4da4caa5a5fbd8a57286c345c2f2, mined in block 277,316 at 23:11:54 UTC on 27 December 2013. Changing the flag byte to NONE makes it fail. The signature is also an example of the older ECDSA style: its R value begins with 0x88, so a padding zero makes it 72 bytes, which a modern Bitcoin Core avoids by grinding for a small R.

lecture.title: Chapter 8: Digital Signatures
lecture.say: This deck explains how a Bitcoin signature works and what it commits to. Every number on a result picture was computed with the chapter's own Python library. Bitcoin Core 31.1.0 was run once on a test network, and its answers are only read back.
lecture.takeaway: What a signature proves and commits to, how Schnorr and ECDSA work, and what moved since print

lecture.title: Today's route
lecture.say: The route has seven parts that follow the order of the chapter. Three true stories and twenty code examples are spread across them. The examples are listed in the same order in the chapter code tab of the course page, so every listing here can be run and edited there.
lecture.takeaway: Seven parts, twenty examples, three true stories

lecture.title: The questions this chapter answers
lecture.say: The seven questions are the chapter's own, rewritten so that each has an answer on a slide. We return to them in the summary. A reader who can answer all seven has understood the chapter.
lecture.takeaway: Each has an answer on a slide; we return to them in the summary

lecture.title: One chapter, seven parts
lecture.say: The chapter has seven parts and 45 key concepts. Each part gets a divider, concept cards with everyday comparisons, code that runs, and some parts a true story. The deck follows the order of the chapter.
lecture.takeaway: Seven parts; every slide today lives on this map

lecture.title: Foundations of digital signatures
lecture.say: A digital signature is a proof that the holder of a private key approved a message. This part shows what verification needs, why two moduli appear, and what is really signed.
lecture.takeaway: A signature is a wax seal that only the owner of the ring can press.

lecture.title: Foundations of digital signatures (1 of 2)
lecture.say: These cards cover Digital Signatures, How Digital Signatures Work and Creating a Digital Signature. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 8.
lecture.takeaway: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

lecture.title: Three inputs, one answer
lecture.say: Verification takes a message, a public key and a signature, and answers yes or no. We flip one bit of the message, then swap the key, and both attempts fail. Only the true triple passes. It is example 1 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
lecture.takeaway: Change the message, the key or the signature and the answer turns to False

lecture.title: Foundations of digital signatures (2 of 2)
lecture.say: These cards cover Verifying the Signature and discrete logarithm problem. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 8.
lecture.takeaway: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

lecture.title: Scalars wrap at n, coordinates at p
lecture.say: The signature equation lives in the group of curve points, whose order is n. Reducing the response modulo n makes the equation hold, reducing it modulo p does not. The two numbers differ by 129 bits. It is example 2 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
lecture.takeaway: The book says everything is modulo p; the response is reduced modulo n

lecture.title: What is signed is a digest
lecture.say: A signature is made over a hash of selected transaction fields. The same transaction gives the same digest, and raising one output by a satoshi gives a completely different one, so the signature no longer fits. It is example 3 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
lecture.takeaway: The signature covers a hash of the transaction, not the bytes themselves

lecture.title: Signature hash flags (SIGHASH)
lecture.say: A signature need not cover the whole transaction. One byte, the SIGHASH flag, chooses what it covers. We measure what each flag commits to and meet the bug of SINGLE.
lecture.takeaway: A flag chooses how much of the letter the seal covers.

lecture.title: Signature hash flags (SIGHASH) (1 of 2)
lecture.say: These cards cover Signature Hash Types (SIGHASH), signature hash, SIGHASH_ALL and SIGHASH_NONE. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 8.
lecture.takeaway: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

lecture.title: A flag is one byte
lecture.say: The flag appended to a signature is a single byte. The three base flags are 1, 2 and 3. The modifier ANYONECANPAY is 128, the top bit, which is why it can be added to any base flag. It is example 4 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
lecture.takeaway: ANYONECANPAY is the top bit, so it combines with every base flag

lecture.title: Signature hash flags (SIGHASH) (2 of 2)
lecture.say: These cards cover SIGHASH_SINGLE, SIGHASH_ANYONECANPAY, BIP118 and SIGHASH_DEFAULT. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 8.
lecture.takeaway: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

lecture.title: What each flag commits to
lecture.say: We change one field of the transaction at a time and ask if the digest moves. ALL covers all five probed fields. The other flags leave some open, which is what lets others complete a transaction. It is example 5 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
lecture.takeaway: Only plain ALL covers every probed field, other inputs' sequences included

lecture.title: SINGLE with no matching output
lecture.say: SIGHASH_SINGLE signs the output with the same number as the input. For inputs one and two there is none, so the legacy algorithm signs the constant one, which holds for any transaction. It is example 6 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
lecture.takeaway: A digest equal to the number one can be reused on any transaction

lecture.title: Schnorr signatures
lecture.say: Schnorr signatures began as a proof of identity. We turn the proof into a signature, meet the BIP340 format, and see why keys that add up bring both multisignatures and a trap.
lecture.takeaway: Schnorr is a seal whose imprints can be added together.

lecture.title: Schnorr signatures: key concepts (1 of 4)
lecture.say: These cards cover Schnorr Signatures, Serialization of Schnorr Signatures, Schnorr-based Scriptless Multisignatures and Schnorr-based Scriptless Threshold Signatures. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 8.
lecture.takeaway: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

lecture.title: The protocol with whole numbers
lecture.say: The book teaches the protocol with whole numbers first. The proof works: s times G equals the commitment plus the challenge times the public key. But dividing the public key by G reveals the secret. It is example 7 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
lecture.takeaway: With plain integers anyone divides and reads the secret; points forbid that

lecture.title: Schnorr signatures: key concepts (2 of 4)
lecture.say: These cards cover challenge, Fiat-Shamir transform, BIP340 and x-only public key. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 8.
lecture.takeaway: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

lecture.title: From identity proof to signature
lecture.say: An honest prover's response passes and a wrong one fails. Letting a hash of the message choose the challenge turns the proof into a signature, and the signature fits only that message. It is example 8 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
lecture.takeaway: The hash of the message plays the examiner, so no examiner has to be online

lecture.title: The signature that was patented for two decades
lecture.say: This is a true story, dated 1991-02-19. Claus-Peter Schnorr published an efficient identification and signature scheme for smart cards in the proceedings of the Crypto '89 conference, and the United States published his patent 4,995,082 on 19 February 1991, filed on 23 February 1990 and claiming priority from 24 February 1989.
lecture.takeaway: A patent decided which signature Bitcoin started with

lecture.title: Schnorr signatures: key concepts (3 of 4)
lecture.say: These cards cover linearity, batch verification, key prefixing and scriptless multisignature. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 8.
lecture.takeaway: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

lecture.title: A fixed size: 64 bytes
lecture.say: A BIP340 public key is the x coordinate only, 32 bytes. The signature is 64 bytes, always. The ECDSA signature of the same key is written in DER, whose length varies by a byte or two. It is example 9 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
lecture.takeaway: Schnorr is smaller and of fixed size; DER signatures vary

lecture.title: Schnorr signatures: key concepts (4 of 4)
lecture.say: These cards cover key cancellation attack, MuSig2, Shamir secret sharing and scriptless threshold signature. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 8.
lecture.takeaway: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

lecture.title: A key that cancels another key
lecture.say: If keys are simply added, Bob can wait for Alice's key and publish a key that cancels it. Then Bob alone signs for both. With MuSig2's hashed weights the same attack no longer gives Bob's key. It is example 10 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
lecture.takeaway: MuSig2 weights each key by a hash of all keys, which stops the trick

lecture.title: Any two of three shares
lecture.say: A secret is the height of a line at zero. Each of three shares is a point on that line. Any two points rebuild the line and give the secret, while one share alone fits every possible secret. It is example 11 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
lecture.takeaway: Fewer than the threshold reveal nothing; the threshold reveals everything

lecture.title: ECDSA signatures
lecture.say: ECDSA signed every Bitcoin payment from 2009 and still signs most. We run its formulas, take apart its byte layout and separate what miners enforce from what nodes prefer.
lecture.takeaway: ECDSA is the older seal, with a messier imprint and two valid shapes.

lecture.title: ECDSA signatures: key concepts (1 of 2)
lecture.say: These cards cover ECDSA Signatures, ECDSA Algorithm, Serialization of ECDSA Signatures (DER) and ECDSA. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 8.
lecture.takeaway: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

lecture.title: ECDSA with the book's formulas
lecture.say: We sign with an explicit nonce and verify by rebuilding the point K. The second valid value of s is n minus s. Nodes relay only the smaller one, the low form. It is example 12 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
lecture.takeaway: If s verifies, so does n minus s: the signature has two forms

lecture.title: ECDSA signatures: key concepts (2 of 2)
lecture.say: These cards cover R and s, malleability, DER and low-S rule. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 8.
lecture.takeaway: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

lecture.title: Nine elements in 71 bytes
lecture.say: DER writes the signature as nested fields: a type, a length, then R and s, each with its own tag and length, and a final hash-type byte. The byte counts add up to the signature. It is example 13 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
lecture.takeaway: Seven of the nine elements are one byte; R and s take 32 each

lecture.title: The signature on the page is a real payment
lecture.say: This is a true story, dated 2013-12-27. The long hexadecimal string that chapter 8 of Mastering Bitcoin uses to explain the DER layout, beginning 3045022100884d142d, is not an invented example: it is the signature in the input of transaction 0627052b6f28912f2703066a912ea577f2ce4da4caa5a5fbd8a57286c345c2f2, mined in block 277,316 at 23:11:54 UTC on 27 December 2013.
lecture.takeaway: The signature printed in the book is a real payment

lecture.title: Valid for miners, refused by nodes
lecture.say: Both forms of the signature verify, so a block that contains the high-S twin is valid. A node, however, relays only the low form. Policy is stricter than consensus, and can be changed without a fork. It is example 14 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
lecture.takeaway: Policy is a stricter house rule; consensus is the law

lecture.title: Policy or consensus?
lecture.say: High S is policy: miners accept it, nodes do not relay it. Strict DER became consensus in 2015. Keeping the two apart explains why a transaction can be valid and yet never reach a miner through ordinary nodes.
lecture.takeaway: Policy can change with a release; consensus changes only by a fork

lecture.title: Randomness and signature size
lecture.say: A signature needs a number used once. If it repeats, the key leaks; if it is derived from key and message, it never repeats. The part ends with how it changes the signature size.
lecture.takeaway: The nonce is a one-time pad: use it twice and the secret leaks.

lecture.title: Randomness and signature size: key concepts
lecture.say: These cards cover The Importance of Randomness in Signatures, nonce, RFC 6979 and nonce reuse. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 8.
lecture.takeaway: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

lecture.title: One nonce, two signatures, no secret
lecture.say: Two signatures with the same nonce give two equations in two unknowns. Subtracting them reveals the nonce and then the private key. A different nonce for the second message leaves nothing to solve. It is example 15 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
lecture.takeaway: Android's weak generator made this attack possible in 2013

lecture.title: When the phone's random numbers were not random
lecture.say: This is a true story, dated 2013-08-11. On 11 August 2013 Bitcoin.org published an alert that the Android component that generates secure random numbers contained critical weaknesses, which made every wallet generated on Android vulnerable to theft, and named Bitcoin Wallet, blockchain.info, BitcoinSpinner and Mycelium Wallet; Bitcoin Wallet 3.15 rotated keys automatically.
lecture.takeaway: Weak randomness at signing time gives away the key

lecture.title: The nonce derived from the key
lecture.say: RFC 6979 derives the nonce by keyed hashing of the secret key and the message. It never repeats for different messages, and a signature can be repeated and compared exactly in a test. It is example 16 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
lecture.takeaway: Same key and message always give the same nonce, and so the same signature

lecture.title: About half are one byte longer
lecture.say: When the top bit of R is set, DER adds a zero byte, so the signature has 71 bytes instead of 70. Over 200 signatures about half are longer. Core grinds the nonce to avoid the extra byte. It is example 17 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
lecture.takeaway: Bitcoin Core signs again until R is small, to save a byte

lecture.title: Segwit signing
lecture.say: Segregated witness changed what is hashed when a transaction is signed. We count the bytes of the old and the new method and see why the amount is now part of the signature.
lecture.takeaway: Segwit changed what is signed, as a cheque that also states the amount.

lecture.title: Segwit signing: key concepts
lecture.say: These cards cover Segregated Witness's New Signing Algorithm, BIP143, O(n) hashing and taproot signature. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 8.
lecture.takeaway: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

lecture.title: Quadratic hashing
lecture.say: The old algorithm hashes almost the whole transaction again for every input. BIP143 hashes the shared parts once. The ratio of the two grows with the number of inputs. It is example 18 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
lecture.takeaway: Doubling the inputs roughly quadruples the bytes the old method hashes

lecture.title: BIP143 signs the amount
lecture.say: In the old algorithm the signer never saw the value of the coin it spent. In BIP143 the amount is part of the digest, so a wrong amount gives a different digest and an invalid signature. It is example 19 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
lecture.takeaway: The new digest changes with the amount; the old one cannot

lecture.title: Since the book went to print
lecture.say: The book went to print in 2023 and the standards have moved. This part collects the dates, the status of the proposals and the evidence trail behind every number in the deck.
lecture.takeaway: Standards move on after print, like a map that needs a new edition.

lecture.title: Dates behind the patent and taproot
lecture.say: United States law gave the longer of 17 years from grant or 20 years from filing. For Schnorr's patent that ends on 23 February 2010. Taproot activated 4,698 days after the genesis block. It is example 20 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
lecture.takeaway: The patent ended in 2010; taproot came eleven years later

lecture.title: Status of the BIPs the chapter names
lecture.say: The book states what was a draft in 2023. Counting the saved index of proposals shows six deployed, two complete, four drafts and one closed. A draft can still change, so check the index before you rely on a number.
lecture.takeaway: A proposal's status can change after print; check the index

lecture.title: The chapter in five lines
lecture.say: These five lines are the deck in miniature, one for each group of parts. A line that feels unproven should send you back to its code slide, because every figure in it was computed there. The chapter code tab of the course page reruns all twenty examples.
lecture.takeaway: If a line feels unproven, the code slide of its part carries the receipt

lecture.title: Where to go from here
lecture.say: Everything here is free to read or watch, and every link was opened on the date in the subtitle. A good start is the Optech workshop on Schnorr and taproot, then BIP340 read beside the chapter. The course page for chapter 8 carries the full text.

examples.name: Policy is stricter than consensus
examples.code:

twin = L.der_encode(r, L.N - s)

ver = lambda g: L.ecdsa_verify(pk, K.MSG, g)
low = lambda g: L.is_low_s(g + b'\x01')
verdict = [(ver(g), low(g)) for g in (sig, twin)]
